name: PIC18F25K80T-I_SS
title: PIC18F66K80 family: 8-bit PIC18 microcontrollers with ECAN, 32 or 64 Kbytes Flash, 1.8 V to 5.5 V, up to 64 MHz
summary: An 8-bit PIC18 microcontroller family in 28, 40, 44 and 64-pin packages, clocked at up to 64 MHz, with 32 or 64 Kbytes of self-programmable Flash, 3,648 bytes of SRAM and 1,024 bytes of data EEPROM. Each member carries an ECAN controller (CAN 2.0B active, up to 1 Mbps), two EUSARTs with LIN/J2602 support, one MSSP (SPI or I2C), a differential 12-bit A/D of 8 or 11 channels, two comparators, a CTMU, four CCP and one ECCP module and five timers, with Run, Idle and Sleep power-managed modes (Sleep down to 13 nA typical). PIC18F devices run from 1.8 V to 5.5 V through an on-chip core regulator; PIC18LF devices run from 1.8 V to 3.6 V. PIC18F25K80T-I/SS is the 32 Kbyte, 28-pin SSOP PIC18F part on tape and reel, for -40 °C to +85 °C, with 24 I/O pins.

circuits.title: Recommended minimum connections (28-pin SSOP)

C7 is 10 µF on parts with the regulator enabled; PIC18LF parts, whose regulator is off, take 0.1 µF on VCAP/VDDCORE.
VCAP/VDDCORE is never tied to VDD. Its trace to C7 is at most 6 mm (0.25 inch).

circuits.title: MCLR pin connections with a jumper
circuits.description: MCLR pulled up to VDD by R1 through series resistor R2, with the filter capacitor C1 hung on the pull-up node through jumper JP so that C1 can be lifted off while a programmer or debugger drives MCLR and refitted for normal running.

parts.note: limits current from C1 into MCLR if the pin breaks down under ESD or EOS

notes: R1 and R2 must still let MCLR meet its VIH and VIL limits.
Parts on the MCLR pin sit within 6 mm (0.25 inch) of it.

circuits.title: RC oscillator mode
circuits.description: External RC oscillator: REXT from VDD and CEXT to VSS meet at OSC1 and set the frequency; OSC2/CLKO puts out the oscillator frequency divided by four.
notes: The frequency depends on supply voltage, REXT, CEXT and temperature, and varies from unit to unit.

circuits.title: RCIO oscillator mode
circuits.description: The RC oscillator with OSC2 freed: REXT and CEXT on OSC1 set the frequency, and the OSC2 pin works as general-purpose I/O RA6.

circuits.title: Crystal or ceramic resonator operation (HS or HSPLL)
circuits.description: A parallel-resonant crystal or a ceramic resonator between OSC1 and OSC2 with a load capacitor from each side to ground; RS in series with OSC2 is fitted when the crystal needs it. The feedback resistor RF is inside the device and changes with the oscillator mode.

parts.note: crystal: 27 pF at 4 MHz, 22 pF at 8 MHz, 15 pF at 20 MHz; resonator: 27 pF at 8 MHz, 22 pF at 16 MHz
may be needed for AT strip-cut crystals

notes: A series-resonant crystal may oscillate off its specified frequency.
Load capacitors sit next to the crystal on the device's side of the board, the whole circuit within 12 mm (0.5 inch) of the oscillator pins.

circuits.title: External clock input operation (EC)
circuits.description: An external clock drives OSC1/CLKI; OSC2/CLKO carries the clock divided by four for test or to synchronise other logic. No oscillator start-up time follows a Power-on Reset or a wake from Sleep.

circuits.title: External clock input operation (HS oscillator configuration)
circuits.description: An external clock into OSC1 with the device set for HS mode; OSC2 is left open and gives no divide-by-four output. The oscillator's feedback circuit stays on, so the current is somewhat higher than in EC mode.

circuits.title: Ultra low-power wake-up
circuits.description: A capacitor on RA0/ULPWU through a series resistor. Firmware charges it with RA0 driven high, turns RA0 to an input, enables the ULPWU current sink and sleeps; the device wakes when the falling capacitor voltage crosses VIL. The RC discharge time sets the wake-up period. The resistor limits current into the pin and lets the time-out be calibrated in software.

circuits.title: External Power-on Reset circuit for slow VDD power-up
circuits.description: An RC delay on MCLR for a supply that rises too slowly for the internal POR: R charges C from VDD, R1 feeds the node into MCLR, and diode D empties C quickly when VDD falls.

parts.note: keeps the drop across R within the device's specification
limits current from C into MCLR if the pin breaks down under ESD or EOS

notes: Used only where VDD ramps up too slowly for the internal POR.

circuits.title: Open-drain output with an external pull-up (USART transmit)
circuits.description: A peripheral output (the EUSART transmit pin in this example) set to open-drain through ODCON, with a resistor pulling the line up to an outside rail. The device runs from VDD while the line swings to the rail of the pull-up, so it can talk to logic on another supply.
notes: U1OD and U2OD set open-drain on the EUSART outputs; SSPOD and CCPxOD do the same for SPI and the CCP outputs.

circuits.title: External components for the SOSC oscillator
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz watch crystal across SOSCI and SOSCO, a 12 pF capacitor from each side to ground. The oscillator clocks Timer1 and Timer3 or the device, and keeps running in every power-managed mode.
notes: 12 pF suits a crystal rated CL = 10 pF with SOSCSEL<1:0> = 11 (higher drive level).
In the low drive level mode (SOSCSEL<1:0> = 01) only about 3 pF to 10 pF per pin is allowed.

Place the circuit close to the device with nothing but VSS or VDD running inside its outline; a grounded guard ring helps next to fast signals, and RC2 toggling as an output can upset the oscillator in the low drive mode.

circuits.title: CTMU current source calibration
circuits.description: A precision resistor from an otherwise unused analog input to ground. With the CTMU current source on and steady, the A/D reads the voltage across RCAL and the current is V / RCAL.

parts.note: for 0.55 µA and a 2.31 V reading; 420 kΩ at 5.5 µA, 42 kΩ at 55 µA; 0.1% or better

notes: Any A/D input (ANx) serves; AN2 is the channel the setup routine configures.

circuits.title: CTMU time measurement connections
circuits.description: Two edge inputs start and stop the CTMU current; the charge it leaves on the A/D sample capacitor, plus an optional external capacitor on an analog input, gives the time between the edges.
notes: Any A/D input (ANx) serves.
For the shortest times, select an unused A/D channel with no trace on its pin, so the total stays near the A/D's own 25 pF.

circuits.title: CTMU pulse delay generation
circuits.description: An edge on CTED1 starts the CTMU current charging CDELAY on CTMUI; when the capacitor reaches the comparator 2 trip point (CVREF), or when CTDIN goes high, a pulse appears on CTPLS. CTMUDS picks comparator 2 (clear) or CTDIN (set). An outside comparator watching CDELAY against its own reference can drive CTDIN.
notes: With a capacitive sensor (humidity, for one) as CDELAY the pulse width follows the sensor; a capture input can measure it.

circuits.title: Standard half-bridge (push-pull)
circuits.description: P1A and P1B, through FET drivers, switch an upper and a lower MOSFET whose midpoint drives a load returned to the centre of a split supply. P1B carries the complement of P1A, with the dead-band delay in ECCP1DEL keeping both switches from conducting at once.

parts.note: upper half of the split supply
lower half of the split supply

circuits.title: Half-bridge outputs driving a full bridge
circuits.description: Two PWM signals run four switches: P1A drives the upper-left and lower-right MOSFETs, P1B the lower-left and upper-right, each through its own FET driver, with the load across the bridge.

circuits.title: Full-bridge application
circuits.description: Four outputs, each through a FET driver, run an H-bridge between V+ and V-: P1A drives QA (upper left), P1B QB (lower left), P1C QC (upper right), P1D QD (lower right). In forward mode P1A holds QA on while P1D modulates QD; in reverse mode P1C holds QC on while P1B modulates QB.
notes: Full-bridge mode has no dead-band delay. Reversing at or near 100% duty with switches that turn off slower than they turn on lets shoot-through current flow in QC and QD (or QA and QB); cut the duty for one period before reversing, or use drivers that turn the switches off faster than on.

circuits.title: SPI master/slave connection
circuits.description: Two of these microcontrollers joined over SPI. Processor 1 runs as master (SSPM<3:0> = 00xxb) and drives the serial clock; processor 2 runs as slave (SSPM<3:0> = 010xb). Each SDO feeds the other's SDI, so a byte shifts out of each shift register on one clock edge and is latched on the other, and both devices exchange a byte per transfer. Both must use the same clock polarity (CKP).
notes: In master mode SDO needs TRISC<5> and SCK TRISC<3> clear; in slave mode SCK needs TRISC<3> set and SS (RA5) TRISA<5> set. SDI is controlled by the module.

circuits.title: Comparator voltage reference output buffer
circuits.description: The comparator voltage reference brought out on RA0 (CVROE set), with a capacitor from RA0 to ground and an outside op amp wired as a unity-gain follower. The reference's drive current is limited, so a buffer is needed when CVREF is connected to outside circuits.
notes: The source resistance seen at RA0 depends on CVRCON<3:0> and CVRCON<5>.

circuits.title: Core regulator enabled (PIC18F parts)
circuits.description: On an F part the internal regulator feeds the 3.3 V core from a VDD rail of 5 V. The VDDCORE/VCAP pin needs a low-ESR filter capacitor CF to ground to keep the regulator stable.

parts.note: low ESR; value from the supply-voltage DC characteristics

notes: 5 V is a typical operating voltage; the full VDD and VDDCORE ranges are in the supply-voltage DC characteristics.

circuits.title: Core regulator disabled (PIC18LF parts)
circuits.description: On an LF part the regulator is off and a 3.3 V VDD powers the core directly; VDDCORE/VCAP still takes a 0.1 µF capacitor to ground.
notes: VDD must stay within the VDDCORE limits.
3.3 V is a typical operating voltage; the full ranges are in the supply-voltage DC characteristics.

operation.text: Run, Idle (CPU off, peripherals on) and Sleep (both off) modes, two-speed oscillator start-up, fail-safe clock monitor, peripheral module disable and ultra low-power wake-up. Typical figures: wake-up 1 µs, WDT 300 nA, Run from 3.8 µA, Idle from 880 nA, Sleep from 13 nA. Programmable BOR and LVD, ICSP and in-circuit debug on two pins, two interrupt priority levels, self-programming under software control.

CAN 2.0B active; legacy mode compatible with older PIC18CXX8/FXX8 CAN modules, enhanced mode, and FIFO mode with programmable TX/RX buffers. Up to 1 Mbps, DeviceNet data-byte filtering, six programmable receive/transmit buffers, three dedicated transmit buffers with priority, two dedicated receive buffers, 16 full 29-bit acceptance filters with dynamic association, three full 29-bit masks, automatic remote-frame handling and error management.

Four CCP modules and one ECCP; Timer0 (8 or 16-bit with 8-bit prescaler), Timer1 and Timer3 (16-bit), Timer2 and Timer4 (8-bit). Two comparators, a configurable reference clock output, a CTMU measuring capacitance and time (1 ns typical resolution) with its own voltage reference, an integrated voltage reference. PORTB and PORTC pins sink and source 25 mA; up to four external interrupts. One MSSP (3/4-wire SPI in all four modes, I2C master and slave); two addressable EUSARTs with LIN/J2602 and auto-baud detect; a 12-bit A/D of up to 11 channels with automatic acquisition, operation in Sleep and a differential input mode; a data signal modulator choosing its modulator and carrier from other module outputs.

Twelve devices: PIC18F25K80, PIC18F26K80, PIC18F45K80, PIC18F46K80, PIC18F65K80 and PIC18F66K80, each also as a PIC18LF version. Flash is 32 Kbytes on the x5K80 parts and 64 Kbytes on the x6K80 parts. The 28-pin parts have three bidirectional ports, the 40/44-pin parts five and the 64-pin parts seven; every other feature is the same across the family.

Code can run from Timer1's source or the internal RC oscillator to cut run current, the CPU can be stopped while peripherals keep running (Idle), and the modes are switched by firmware on the fly. XLP adds an extra-low-power BOR and a low-power watchdog.

External RC (RA6 free) or RCIO (clock out); external clock EC (RA6 free) or ECIO (clock out); crystal XT, HS or LP. A PLL multiplies external oscillator modes up to 64 MHz and also works with the internal oscillator. The internal block gives 16 MHz (±2%) and a roughly 31 kHz source stable over temperature and VDD, runs as HF-INTOSC or MF-INTOSC when set for 16 MHz or 500 kHz, and frees both oscillator pins for I/O. It backs the fail-safe clock monitor (switches to the internal oscillator if the main clock fails) and two-speed start-up (runs from the internal oscillator after POR or wake until the primary clock is ready).
Program Flash is rated for 10,000 erase/write cycles with retention estimated above 20 years; it is readable and writable by firmware. Data RAM is up to 3.6 Kbytes.
An optional extension, enabled by a configuration bit, adds eight instructions and an indexed addressing mode, aimed at re-entrant code compiled from high-level languages such as C.

All members share one peripheral set and a consistent pinout across 28, 40, 44 and 64 pins and both memory sizes. The family is largely pin compatible with the PIC18F4580, PIC18F4680 and PIC18F8680 families with ECAN. The low-power WDT has a 22-bit prescaler for a long time-out stable over voltage and temperature.
RA6 and RA7 are digital I/O only in oscillator modes that do not use those pins. RE3 is an input only when MCLR is disabled (MCLRE configuration bit = 0).

Always connected: every VDD and VSS pin, every AVDD and AVSS pin whether or not the analog features are used, MCLR, and ENVREG (where the device has it) and VCAP/VDDCORE. Connected when used: PGC/PGD for ICSP and debugging, OSCI/OSCO for an external oscillator, VREF+/VREF- for an external analog reference.

Each supply pair (VDD/VSS, AVDD/AVSS) takes a 0.1 µF (100 nF), 10-20 V low-ESR ceramic resonant at 200 MHz or higher, as close to the pins as possible and on the device's side of the board; through a via on another layer the trace from pin to capacitor stays within 6 mm (0.25 inch). For noise in the tens of MHz and above, a second ceramic of 0.01 µF to 0.001 µF goes beside each primary one (for example 0.1 µF with 0.001 µF). Power and return traces reach the capacitors before the device pins, and the capacitor-to-pin traces are kept short.

Where power traces run longer than six inches, a local tank capacitor sized from the trace resistance and the peak current for an acceptable voltage sag supplies the device; typical values 4.7 µF to 47 µF.

MCLR serves device Reset and programming/debugging. Without programming needs it may go straight to VDD; added parts can improve immunity to Resets from supply sags. Programmers and debuggers drive MCLR, so R1 and C1 must not spoil its VIH/VIL levels or fast edges; C1 can be isolated with a jumper during programming. Parts on MCLR sit within 6 mm (0.25 inch) of the pin.

Where a device has ENVREG, it is tied directly to a supply (regulator on) or to ground (regulator off). With the regulator on, VCAP/VDDCORE needs a 10 µF low-ESR (< 5 Ω) ceramic or tantalum capacitor to ground, never a connection to VDD, with a trace no longer than 6 mm (0.25 inch). With the regulator off, VCAP/VDDCORE is tied to a supply at the VDDCORE level. PIC18LF devices have the regulator permanently off, no ENVREG pin, need 0.1 µF on VCAP/VDDCORE and must meet the regulator-disabled VDD limit of parameter D001. Devices with the regulator permanently on also lack ENVREG and still need the 10 µF capacitor.

X5R and X7R parts start at ±10% to ±20% and drift about ±15% over temperature; Y5V parts start at -20%/+80% and drift +22%/-82%, so a 10 µF Y5V part may fall below what the regulator needs for stability and transient response and is not recommended over a wide temperature range. Capacitance also falls with DC bias, so pick a voltage rating well above the working voltage, for example 16 V for the 2.5 V core.

Keep the traces from the ICSP connector to PGC and PGD short. Where the connector may take ESD, a series resistor of a few tens of ohms, at most 100 Ω, is recommended. Pull-ups, series diodes and capacitors on PGC/PGD interfere with programmer and debugger communication; remove them while programming, or meet the loading and VIH/VIL limits of the Flash programming specification. The Communication Channel Select programmed into the device must match the PGCx/PGDx pins wired to the debugger.

Place the oscillator circuit on the device's side of the board within 12 mm (0.5 inch) of its pins, load capacitors beside the crystal. Surround it with a grounded copper pour returned directly to the MCU ground, with no signal or power traces inside the pour, and none on the opposite side under the crystal on a two-sided board. Fine-pitch packages that cannot be fully ringed tie the broken guard to a mirrored ground layer. Neighbouring port pins and signals near the oscillator should be quiet: no high frequencies or fast edges.
Configure unused pins as outputs driven low, or tie each to VSS through 1 kΩ to 10 kΩ and drive it low.

Modes: EC, ECIO (FOSC/4 on RA6), HS, XT, LP, RC, RCIO (FOSC/4 on RA6), INTIO2 (I/O on RA6 and RA7) and INTIO1 (FOSC/4 on RA6, I/O on RA7), chosen by FOSC<3:0> (CONFIG1H<3:0>). Primary-oscillator bias is set by input frequency: low power below 160 kHz, medium from 160 kHz to 16 MHz, high above 16 MHz. HS1 covers 4 MHz to 16 MHz (medium power) and HS2 16 MHz to 25 MHz (high power); EC1 runs up to 160 kHz, EC2 160 kHz to 16 MHz, EC3 16 MHz to 64 MHz.

The PLL runs on any clock source with an input of 4 MHz to 16 MHz. In EC and HS modes PLLCFG (CONFIG1H<4>) or PLLEN (OSCTUNE<6>) enables it. With HF-INTOSC (FOSC<3:0> = 100x) only PLLEN enables it, PLLCFG is ignored, and the PLL can be on only when HF-INTOSC is at 4, 8 or 16 MHz. RA6 and RA7 not used by the oscillator or CLKOUT are general-purpose I/O.

Three independent sources: primary oscillators on OSC1/OSC2 (crystal, resonator and external clock modes, or the internal block when FOSC selects it), secondary oscillators off those pins, and the internal block (31 kHz LF-INTOSC, 31 kHz to 500 kHz MF-INTOSC, 31 kHz to 16 MHz HF-INTOSC). LF-INTOSC also clocks the WDT and fail-safe clock monitor. Crystal modes (XT, HS, LP) have a built-in start-up time; EC and EXTRC start at once.

The SOSC (Timer1/3/5/7 oscillator) keeps running in power-managed modes. It is started when an odd timer selects it through its SOSCEN bit (TxCON<3>), when SCS<1:0> selects it as CPU clock, or when SOSCGO (OSCCON2<3>) is set, which warms it up before a peripheral asks for it. SOSCSEL<1:0> (CONFIG1L<4:3>) picks high-power, low-power or digital (SCLKI) operation; for digital I/O on RC0 and RC1 without an SOSC, set the digital mode. The Timer oscillator must be enabled and should be stable before a SLEEP that switches to it, otherwise the switch is ignored or a long delay may follow.

SCS<1:0> (OSCCON<1:0>) choose the primary clock defined by FOSC<3:0>, the secondary SOSC clock or the internal oscillator; the switch follows a short transition after the write. OSTS (OSCCON<3>) shows the primary clock running after the OST, SOSCRUN (OSCCON2<6>) the SOSC clocking the device; at most one is set in power-managed modes, and neither means INTOSC is clocking or not yet stable. IDLEN (OSCCON<7>) decides whether SLEEP enters Sleep or an Idle mode.

Every Reset clears SCS, so the FOSC-defined primary clock runs after Reset. When the internal block without PLL is the Reset clock, INTOSC starts at 8 MHz (IRCF<2:0> = 110). INTOSC always runs at power-up until the configuration is loaded, then the FOSC setting takes over. Clock switching is glitch-free; the pause is two cycles of the old clock plus three to four of the new one, if the new one is stable.

For timing-insensitive designs. Frequency depends on supply voltage, REXT, CEXT and temperature, and varies unit to unit with manufacturing spread, package lead-frame capacitance (most for small CEXT) and component tolerance. In RC mode OSC2 carries FOSC/4; in RCIO mode OSC2 is RA6. Recommended REXT 3 kΩ to 100 kΩ, CEXT 20 pF to 300 pF.
In HS or HSPLL the crystal or resonator connects across OSC1 and OSC2 and must be parallel-resonant. The capacitor tables are starting points; test over the VDD and temperature range of the design.

EC and ECPLL take an external clock on OSC1 and need no start-up time after POR or Sleep; in EC mode OSC2 outputs FOSC/4. An external clock may also feed OSC1 in HS mode, with no FOSC/4 output and slightly higher current, as the feedback circuit stays enabled (it is off in EC).

HSPLL and ECPLL multiply an external source by four, giving up to 64 MHz, enabled by PLLEN (OSCTUNE<6>) or PLLCFG (CONFIG1H<4>). With HF-INTOSC as primary, PLLEN alone controls the PLL, even with PLLCFG = 1, and should be set only with an HF-INTOSC output of 4 MHz to 16 MHz (postscaler at 4, 8 or 16 MHz); the result is up to 64 MHz. The PLL suits a low-frequency crystal (less EMI) or full speed from the internal oscillator.

Three sources: HF-INTOSC, MF-INTOSC and LF-INTOSC. HF-INTOSC gives 31 kHz to 16 MHz through the IRCF<2:0> postscaler; with the PLL its input must be 4 MHz to 16 MHz (IRCF = 111, 110 or 101). INTSRC (OSCTUNE<7>) and MFIOSEL (OSCCON2<0>) choose which source gives 31 kHz to 500 kHz: HF-INTOSC with INTSRC = 1 and MFIOSEL = 0, MF-INTOSC with both set; with INTSRC = 0 only LF-INTOSC's 31 kHz is offered. LF-INTOSC turns on by itself when the PWRT, FSCM, WDT or two-speed start-up is enabled. Default frequency after Reset is 8 MHz.

INTIO1: OSC2 (RA6) outputs FOSC/4 and OSC1 is RA7 I/O. INTIO2: OSC1 is RA7 and OSC2 is RA6, both I/O. The 4x PLL works only with HF-INTOSC and gives 16 MHz or 64 MHz, software-controlled by PLLEN and PLLCFG, only with an output of 4 MHz to 16 MHz selected (OSCCON<6:4> = 111, 110 or 101). INTPLL1 looks like INTIO1 at the pins, INTPLL2 like INTIO2.

Factory calibrated to 16 MHz and adjustable with TUN<5:0> (OSCTUNE<5:0>). After a change the HF/MF-INTOSC frequency moves to the new value over some settling time while code keeps running, with no flag. LF-INTOSC runs independently and is not affected by OSCTUNE; drift in one source is not mirrored in the other.

Three ways to decide when and which way to retune: EUSART errors (framing errors mean the clock is fast, so decrement OSCTUNE; data errors suggest slow, so increment); two timers, one on the peripheral clock and one on a fixed reference such as the SOSC, comparing counts at each reference interrupt; or a CCP capture of Timer1/Timer3 between two external events of known period (such as the mains frequency). A count well above expectation means the oscillator is fast (decrement OSCTUNE); well below means slow (increment).

Besides FOSC/4, any oscillator configuration can send a divided clock to the REFO (RC3) pin, controlled by REFOCON: ROON (REFOCON<7>) enables it and RODIV<3:0> picks one of 16 dividers. ROSEL chooses the OSC1/OSC2 oscillator or the current system clock as source; ROSSLP keeps the output running in Sleep (on RE3). Output in Sleep needs ROSSLP and ROSEL both set and an EC or HS clock mode, otherwise the oscillator powers down in Sleep. With ROSEL clear the output follows the system clock through clock switches.

PRI_IDLE leaves the primary oscillator running; every other power-managed mode stops the OSC1 oscillator. SEC_RUN and SEC_IDLE run from the SOSC, which may run in any mode if needed. RC_RUN and RC_IDLE run from the internal block; LF-INTOSC can also keep running for special features in any mode. Sleep stops all clocks and draws only leakage; anything left running in Sleep adds current (INTOSC for the WDT, SOSC for Timer1 or 3). Some features run without a clock, such as an MSSP slave or the INTx pins.

Two timers hold the device in Reset until the supply and the primary clock are stable, so most designs need no external Reset circuit: the power-up timer (about 64 ms, parameter 33, always on) and the oscillator start-up timer, which counts 1,024 oscillator cycles in HS, XT or LP before releasing the clock. A further interval TCSD (parameter 38) follows POR before instructions execute.

Seven modes in three groups: Run, Idle and Sleep. Run and Idle may use the primary, secondary or internal clock; Sleep uses none. ULPWU on RA0 lets a slowly falling voltage wake the device even from Sleep. IDLEN (OSCCON<7>) decides whether the CPU is clocked and SCS<1:0> (OSCCON<1:0>) the clock source. Writing SCS switches source at once (if that source runs), subject to transition delays; SLEEP enters Idle or Sleep according to IDLEN, so often only a SLEEP is needed.

A clock switch takes two cycles of the old source plus three to four of the new. OSTS (OSCCON<3>), HFIOFS (OSCCON<2>) and SOSCRUN (OSCCON2<6>) report the source. With the internal block as FOSC primary, OSTS and HFIOFS/MFIOFS can both be set in PRI_RUN or PRI_IDLE; entering another INTOSC mode at the same frequency clears OSTS. Changing a single IRCF bit at low VDD can select a clock faster than that VDD supports.
Each SLEEP enters the mode IDLEN calls for at that moment; a SLEEP is only the trigger for Sleep or an Idle mode.
The normal full-power mode and the default after Reset unless two-speed start-up is on. OSTS is set; HFIOFS or MFIOFS may be set when the internal block is the primary clock.

SCS<1:0> = 01: the CPU and peripherals run from the SOSC, the primary oscillator stops, SOSCRUN is set and OSTS cleared, giving low power with an accurate clock. With SOSCGO set first, the switch happens at once. Going back to PRI_RUN, the SOSC keeps clocking until the primary clock is ready, then the switch completes, SOSCRUN clears and OSTS sets; IDLEN and SCS are unchanged and the SOSC keeps running.

SCS1 = 1 (keep SCS0 clear for compatibility): the device runs from the INTOSC multiplexer, the primary clock stops and OSTS clears. With LF-INTOSC this is the lowest-power Run mode. IRCF can be changed at any time for an immediate speed change. If the internal block is already the primary clock, RC_RUN adds only switch delays and is not recommended.

With IRCF and INTSRC all clear, the INTOSC output is off, HFIOFS/MFIOFS stay clear and LF-INTOSC clocks the device. Setting IRCF non-zero, or INTSRC or MFIOSEL, turns INTOSC on and sets HFIOFS or MFIOFS once it is stable, after TIOBST (parameter 39); clocks continue meanwhile. Returning to PRI_RUN, the INTOSC multiplexer clocks the device until the primary clock is ready; LF-INTOSC keeps running if the WDT or FSCM is enabled.

IDLEN clear (its Reset state) and SLEEP: the oscillator stops and all clock status bits clear; no clock switch is needed. LF-INTOSC keeps running for the WDT, and the SOSC if enabled. After a wake event (interrupt, Reset or WDT) the device waits for the SCS-selected clock, or runs from the internal block if two-speed start-up or FSCM is enabled; OSTS sets when the primary clock takes over. IDLEN and SCS are unchanged.

IDLEN set and SLEEP: the CPU stops and the peripherals run from the SCS-selected clock; status bits are unchanged. Exits are by interrupt, WDT time-out or Reset; after a wake event the CPU waits TCSD (parameter 38) and resumes on the same clock (waking from RC_IDLE gives RC_RUN). A WDT time-out in any Idle or Sleep mode wakes to the Run mode SCS names.

The primary clock keeps running, so the CPU resumes fastest and on the accurate clock. Enter from PRI_RUN by setting IDLEN and executing SLEEP, or from another Run mode by setting IDLEN, clearing SCS and executing SLEEP. OSTS stays set. On a wake event the CPU waits TCSD and runs from the primary clock.

Peripherals run from the SOSC with the CPU off. Enter from SEC_RUN by setting IDLEN and executing SLEEP, or from another Run mode by setting IDLEN, then SCS = 01, then SLEEP; the primary oscillator stops, OSTS clears and SOSCRUN sets. After a wake event and TCSD the CPU runs from the SOSC.

Peripherals run from the INTOSC multiplexer with the CPU off. Enter from RC_RUN by setting IDLEN and executing SLEEP, or from another Run mode by setting IDLEN, then SCS1, then SLEEP (keep SCS0 clear). IRCF may be raised before SLEEP for a faster clock. The primary oscillator stops and OSTS clears. After a wake event and TCSD the CPU runs from the INTOSC multiplexer; INTOSC keeps running if the WDT or FSCM is enabled.

Two controls cut a peripheral's power: its XXXEN enable bit stops its function but leaves its registers readable and writable; its XXXMD bit in PMD0, PMD1 or PMD2 removes every clock source, bringing its power to the minimum, and disables its registers (writes ignored, reads invalid).

Any enabled interrupt (its enable bit set in INTCONx or PIEx) wakes the device when its flag sets; code jumps to the vector if GIE/GIEH is set, otherwise continues in line. A WDT time-out wakes from Idle or Sleep, but in a Run mode it causes a WDT Reset. SLEEP or CLRWDT clears the WDT and postscaler, drops the selected clock source when FSCM is enabled, and modifies IRCF when the internal block is the clock. A Reset exit waits for the OST (OSTS set) or for INTOSC (HFIOFS/MFIOFS set); with two-speed start-up or FSCM, code may start as soon as the Reset clears, on the internal block, until the primary clock is ready.

No OST runs when waking from PRI_IDLE (the primary clock never stopped) or when the primary clock is not LP, XT, HS or HSPLL (RC, EC and INTIO need none); a fixed TCSD still follows the wake event before execution resumes.

ULPWU on RA0 wakes the device from a slowly falling voltage without extra current: charge the capacitor on RA0 by driving it high, turn RA0 to an input, set ULPEN and ULPSINK in WDTCON to discharge it, select Sleep and enter it. When RA0 falls below VIL the device wakes and runs the next instruction, and ULPLVL (WDTCON<5>) is set to identify the source. The RC discharge time sets the time-out; a timer can measure charge and discharge to calibrate out temperature, voltage and component spread. The feature can also act as a simple programmable LVD or temperature sensor.

Power-on Reset, MCLR Reset in normal operation or in power-managed modes, WDT Reset during execution, configuration mismatch Reset, programmable brown-out Reset, RESET instruction, Stack Full Reset and Stack Underflow Reset. RCON records the source in its low five bits (cleared by the event, set again by firmware) and also holds IPEN (interrupt priority) and SBOREN (software BOR control). PWRT counts on an 11-bit ripple counter clocked from INTOSC (32 µs, 65.5 ms total); the OST counts 1,024 OSC1 cycles on a 10-bit counter.

Holding MCLR low resets the device; a noise filter ignores short pulses. No internal Reset, including the WDT, drives MCLR low. The MCLRE configuration bit can disable MCLR, turning the pin into a digital input.

An on-chip POR pulse occurs when VDD rises above a threshold. Tie MCLR to VDD through 1 kΩ to 10 kΩ to use it with no external RC delay; VDD must rise faster than parameter D004, or use the external RC circuit. Operating conditions (voltage, frequency, temperature) must be met when Reset ends, otherwise hold the device in Reset. POR (RCON<1>) is cleared by every POR, unchanged by other Resets and never set by hardware; firmware sets it after each POR.

Four BOR power modes, chosen by BORPWR<1:0> (CONFIG2L<6:5>): high, medium, low and zero power. High, medium and low compare VDD with the BORV<1:0> level (CONFIG1L<3:2>): 1.8 V, 2 V, 2.7 V or 3 V. Typical IBOR is 200 nA (zero), 750 nA (low) and 3 µA (medium). A BOR re-arms the POR and resets the device; ZPBORMV only re-arms the POR at about 2 V. Lower power means a less accurate trip level. BOREN<1:0> (CONFIG2L<2:1>) and SBOREN (RCON<6>) enable it. Trip levels BVDD (D005), currents and TBOR (parameter 35) are in the electrical characteristics.

BOREN<1:0> = 01 lets firmware turn BOR on and off with SBOREN (reads 0 in other modes), trimming BOR current without reprogramming; the trip level stays set by BORV<1:0>. BOREN<1:0> = 10 keeps BOR under hardware control but switches it off in Sleep and back on in any other mode.
BOR clears on every brown-out or power-on Reset, so read POR and BOR together: with POR set by firmware after each POR, BOR = 0 with POR = 1 means a brown-out occurred.

The configuration registers are compared continuously with complementary shadow registers; a mismatch, such as from an ESD event flipping bits, causes a CM Reset and clears CM (RCON<5>), which no other Reset changes. It acts like an MCLR Reset, and as with every hard Reset the configuration words reload from Flash.

An 11-bit counter on INTOSC gives about 2048 × 32 µs = 65.6 ms, holding the device in Reset while it counts; the delay varies from chip to chip with temperature and process (parameter 33). Clearing PWRTEN enables it.

operation.topic: Oscillator start-up timer and PLL lock
operation.text: The OST adds 1,024 OSC1 cycles after the PWRT so a crystal or resonator is running, only in XT, LP, HS and HSPLL modes and only on POR or exit from most power-managed modes. With the PLL on, a further fixed time-out, TPLL (typically 2 ms), follows the OST so the PLL can lock.

After the POR pulse, the PWRT runs (if enabled), then the OST. In RC mode with the PWRT disabled there is no time-out. As the time-outs start from the POR pulse, holding MCLR low long enough lets them all expire, so raising MCLR starts execution at once, which can synchronise several devices.

Most registers are unaffected by Reset: unknown after POR and unchanged by other Resets; the rest take a Reset state depending on the Reset type. A WDT wake-up counts as a resumption and leaves most registers alone. RI, TO, PD, CM, POR and BOR in RCON identify the Reset type.

Program memory, data RAM and data EEPROM. Program and data memories sit on separate buses (Harvard), so both can be reached at once. The data EEPROM behaves like a peripheral, reached through control registers.
A 21-bit PC addresses a 2-Mbyte space; reads past the implemented memory return 0 (NOP). The Reset vector is at 0000h, the high-priority interrupt vector at 0008h and the low-priority one at 0018h.

21 bits in PCL (readable and writable), PCH (PC<15:8>) and PCU (PC<20:16>); PCH and PCU are loaded through PCLATH and PCLATU on any write to PCL, and a read of PCL copies the upper bytes into the latches. The PC counts bytes; its LSb is fixed at 0 and it steps by two. CALL, RCALL, GOTO and branches write the PC directly without the latches.

Up to 31 calls and interrupts: a 31-word by 21-bit RAM with a 5-bit pointer, outside program and data space. CALL, RCALL and interrupts push; RETURN, RETLW and RETFIE pop (as do ADDULNK and SUBULNK with the extended set). TOSU:TOSH:TOSL give read/write access to the top entry for software stacks; disable global interrupts while touching it. STKPTR resets to 0, which has no RAM behind it.

STKPTR holds the pointer (0 to 31) and the STKFUL and STKUNF flags, cleared by software or POR. On the 31st push STKFUL sets; with STVREN set (the default) the (PC + 2) value is pushed and the device resets with the pointer at 0, with STVREN clear the pointer stays at 31 and further pushes are lost. Popping an empty stack returns 0 to the PC and sets STKUNF, vectoring to the Reset address without resetting the SFRs. PUSH and POP instructions manipulate the top of stack.

operation.topic: Fast register stack and look-up tables
operation.text: A one-level, unreadable stack saves STATUS, WREG and BSR on every interrupt; RETFIE FAST restores them. With both interrupt priorities in use it cannot be trusted for low-priority returns, which must save those registers in software. CALL label, FAST and RETURN FAST use it for subroutines when interrupts do not. Look-up tables in program memory use a computed GOTO (ADDWF PCL with RETLW entries, offset in multiples of two, one byte per word) or table reads (two bytes per word through TBLPTR and TABLAT).

The clock is divided by four into quadrature clocks Q1 to Q4. The PC increments on Q1; an instruction is fetched and latched into the IR in Q4, then decoded and executed in the next Q1 to Q4 (data read in Q2, written in Q4). Fetch and execute overlap, so instructions take one cycle, and those that change the PC take two as the prefetched instruction is flushed.

Instructions are two or four bytes, stored with the LSB at an even address. CALL and GOTO carry a word address written to PC<20:1>; branch offsets count single-word instructions. The standard two-word instructions are CALL, MOVFF, GOTO and LFSR; their second word starts with 1111, which executes as a NOP if reached alone (after a skip).

Static RAM with 12-bit addresses, up to 4,096 bytes in 16 banks of 256. SFRs control the core and peripherals, GPRs hold data; unimplemented locations read 0. The BSR (low four bits used, loaded by MOVLB) supplies the bank for instructions carrying an 8-bit address; MOVFF carries full 12-bit addresses and ignores the BSR. Writes to unimplemented banks are ignored and reads return 0, though STATUS changes as if they had worked.

A 256-byte window reached without the BSR: 00h-5Fh of Bank 0 (Access RAM, GPRs) and 60h-FFh of Bank 15 (SFRs). Instructions with a = 0 use it and ignore the BSR; with a = 1 they use the BSR. It suits fast variables and context saving. GPRs fill upward from 000h, are not initialised by POR and are unchanged by other Resets.

SFRs are static RAM from FFFh downward, filling Bank 15 (F00h to FFFh) and the top of Bank 14 (EF4h to EFFh). Core registers (ALU, Reset, interrupts) and peripheral registers; unused locations read 0.

Holds N, OV, Z, DC and C. When STATUS is the destination of an instruction affecting those bits, the write to them is blocked (CLRF STATUS sets Z and leaves the rest, reading back 000u u1uu); BCF, BSF, SWAPF, MOVFF and MOVWF are the instructions to alter it. C and DC act as borrow and digit borrow in subtraction.

Inherent, literal, direct and indirect, plus indexed literal offset with the extended set (XINST = 1). Direct instructions carry an 8-bit address interpreted with the BSR (a = 1) or in the Access Bank (a = 0, direct forced); d selects the destination: the file register (d = 1) or W (d = 0).

FSR0, FSR1 and FSR2 each hold a 12-bit pointer covering all data memory without banking. INDF0 to INDF2 access the pointed location; POSTDEC, POSTINC and PREINC adjust the whole pointer (with carry from FSRnL into FSRnH) without touching STATUS flags; PLUSW adds signed W (-127 to 128) as an offset. Indirect access to another FSR's virtual registers reads 00h or does nothing; writing through them to an FSR pair stores the value without the increment or decrement.

Program memory is unaffected; five two-word commands are added: ADDFSR, CALLW, MOVSF, MOVSS and SUBFSR. In data memory, instructions with a = 0 and a file address of 5Fh or less use indexed literal offset addressing: the address is an offset added to FSR2. Instructions with a = 1 or addresses of 60h and above work as before. Access RAM 00h-5Fh then maps a window from FSR2 to FSR2 + 5Fh; Bank 0 below 5Fh is reached only through the BSR. The data memory size, linear addressing, SFR map, FSR0/FSR1 indirect addressing and BSR operation do not change.

Readable, writable and erasable in normal operation across the whole VDD range. Reads are one byte at a time; writes and erases work on 64-byte blocks (32 words); user code cannot bulk erase. A write or erase stalls instruction fetch until the internal timer ends it. Values need not be valid instructions; an invalid one executes as a NOP. TBLRD moves program bytes into data RAM and TBLWT loads 64 holding registers through the 8-bit TABLAT; data tables need no word alignment, code does.

EECON1 controls access; EECON2 is not a physical register, reads 0 and takes the unlock sequence. EEPGD selects program memory (1) or data EEPROM (0); CFGS = 1 selects the configuration registers regardless of EEPGD; FREE = 1 makes the next WR an erase; WREN enables writes (clear at power-up); WR starts a write and is cleared by hardware at the end; WRERR flags a write cut short by Reset or attempted wrongly. EEIF (PIR4<6>) sets when a write completes and is cleared in software.

TBLPTRU:TBLPTRH:TBLPTRL form a 22-bit pointer: 21 bits address 2 Mbytes, the 22nd reaches device ID, user ID and configuration bits. TBLRD uses all 22 bits; TBLWT uses TBLPTR<5:0> to pick one of 64 holding registers and TBLPTR<21:6> to pick the 64-byte block programmed or erased.
TBLRD copies the byte at TBLPTR into TABLAT, optionally adjusting TBLPTR; the address LSb picks the high or low byte of the word.

Erase blocks are 32 words (64 bytes); single words cannot be erased. Sequence: load TBLPTR with the row address, set EEPGD, clear CFGS, set WREN and FREE, disable interrupts, write 55h then 0AAh to EECON2, set WR (the CPU stalls for TIW, parameter D133A), re-enable interrupts.

Write blocks are 32 words (64 bytes); single words or bytes cannot be programmed. Sequence: read the 64 bytes to RAM, update them, erase the row, load TBLPTR with the first address, TBLWT the 64 bytes with auto-increment, set EEPGD, clear CFGS, set WREN, disable interrupts, write 55h and 0AAh to EECON2, set WR (stall for TIW, D133A), re-enable interrupts and verify. Holding registers reset to FFh, and FFh leaves a byte unchanged, so single bytes can be changed without loading all 64 as long as no bit goes from 0 to 1. TBLPTR must point inside the 64-byte range before WR. The write/erase voltages come from an on-chip charge pump rated over the device's voltage range.

Verify written values where heavy writing may stress bits near their limits. After an interrupted write (power loss, unexpected Reset) verify and reprogram the location; after an MCLR or WDT Reset during a write, WRERR flags it. The unlock sequence protects against spurious writes.

A 1,024-byte non-volatile array (address 00h to 3FFh in EEADRH:EEADR, upper six bits of EEADRH ignored), separate from RAM and program memory and reached through EECON1, EECON2, EEDATA, EEADR and EEADRH. It is readable and writable across the whole VDD range, byte by byte, with automatic erase-before-write; write time is set by an on-chip timer and varies with voltage, temperature and chip (parameter D122). RD and WR start reads and writes and are cleared by hardware; RD cannot be set with EEPGD = 1.

operation.topic: Reading and writing the data EEPROM
operation.text: Read: load the address, clear EEPGD, set RD; data is in EEDATA after one cycle (readable after one NOP) and stays until the next read or write. Write: load address and data, set WREN, then for each byte write 55h and 0AAh to EECON2 and set WR, preferably with interrupts disabled; the write does not start otherwise. EECON1, the address and EEDATA cannot change once a write starts; WR and WREN cannot be set in the same instruction. At completion WR clears and EEIF sets (clear it in software). WREN is not cleared by hardware and should stay clear except while updating. Self-writes to Flash and EEPROM cannot run in LP oscillator mode; a self-write switches the device to high-power mode.

EEPROM code-protect bits block external reads and writes, while the device itself can always read and write it. WREN clears at power-up and writes are blocked during the power-up timer (TPWRT, parameter 33); with the unlock sequence this guards against brown-out, glitches and runaway code. The array suits often-changing data; values changed less often than parameter D124 call for an array refresh, so rarely-changed constants belong in Flash.

Part of the ALU: an unsigned 8 x 8 multiply in one instruction cycle, result in PRODH:PRODL, no STATUS flags changed. MULWF does it in one instruction when one operand is in WREG. Signed results need sign-bit tests and subtractions; 16 x 16 products are built from four 8 x 8 multiplies into RES3:RES0.

Most interrupt sources can be given high or low priority. High-priority requests vector to 0008h and can interrupt a low-priority handler; low-priority requests vector to 0018h and wait while a high-priority handler runs. Control sits in RCON, INTCON, INTCON2, INTCON3 and PIR1-PIR5, PIE1-PIE5, IPR1-IPR5. A source normally has a flag bit (the event happened), an enable bit and a priority bit. IPEN (RCON<7>) = 1 turns priority on: GIEH (INTCON<7>) enables the high-priority sources and GIEL (INTCON<6>) the low ones. IPEN = 0 (default) is the mid-range compatible mode: priority bits do nothing, PEIE (INTCON<6>) gates the peripheral sources, GIE (INTCON<7>) gates everything and all requests go to 0008h.

On a response the active global enable (GIE, or GIEH/GIEL) clears, the return address goes on the stack and the PC loads 0008h or 0018h. The handler finds the source by polling flags, which must be cleared in software before interrupts are enabled again, or the interrupt repeats. RETFIE returns and sets the global enable again. Latency for external events (INTx pins, PORTB change) is three to four instruction cycles, the same for one- and two-cycle instructions. Flags set whatever the state of their enable bits or GIE. MOVFF must not change interrupt control registers while any interrupt is enabled; it can make the device misbehave.
Every source in the interrupt logic, peripheral flags as well as TMR0, RBIF and INT0-INT3, can wake the device from Idle or Sleep when its enable bit is set.

INT0-INT3 on RB0-RB3 are edge-triggered: INTEDGx (INTCON2) = 1 selects the rising edge, 0 the falling edge. A valid edge sets INTxIF; INTxIE enables it, and the flag is cleared in software before re-enabling. With INTxIE set before entering a power-managed mode, any of the four wakes the device, and with GIE set the device then branches to the vector. INT1IP (INTCON3<6>), INT2IP (INTCON3<7>) and INT3IP (INTCON2<1>) set priority; INT0 has no priority bit and is always high priority.

Timer0 overflow (FFh to 00h in 8-bit mode, FFFFh to 0000h in 16-bit mode) sets TMR0IF; TMR0IE (INTCON<5>) enables it and TMR0IP (INTCON2<2>) sets its priority. A change on RB7:RB4 sets RBIF (INTCON<0>), enabled by RBIE (INTCON<3>) and per pin by IOCB<7:4>, priority from RBIP (INTCON2<0>).

The return address goes on the stack and WREG, STATUS and BSR are copied to the fast return stack. Without a fast return the handler saves WREG, STATUS and BSR itself (and anything else it changes) and restores them before RETFIE.

Up to seven ports, depending on the device. Each has TRIS (direction), PORT (reads the pin levels) and LAT (the output latch). Writing PORT writes LAT; read-modify-write on LAT works on the latched values. TRIS bit = 1 makes the pin an input with its driver off; 0 makes it an output driving its LAT bit. An enabled peripheral usually takes its pin away from general I/O. Every digital port tolerates 5.5 V on its inputs, and analog ports do too, with internal clamp diodes; every I/O pin has diodes to VDD and VSS.

PORTA, PORTB and PORTC have the stronger drivers, meant for loads such as LEDs. PORTD and PORTE (not on 28-pin) and PORTF and PORTG (64-pin only) drive less: ordinary logic loads and low-current LEDs. PORTB, PORTD, PORTE, PORTF and PORTG have weak pull-ups on every pin, one control bit per port: PORTB uses RBPU (INTCON2<7>); PORTD-PORTG use PADCFG1<7:4> (RDPU, REPU, RFPU, RGPU). WPUB enables PORTB pull-ups pin by pin.

Open-drain drive is available on the USART data and clock pins, the SPI pins of the MSSP and the CCP outputs, selected by one ODCON bit each (SSPOD, CCP5OD-CCP1OD, U2OD, U1OD), so they can drive a line pulled to another voltage. An open-drain output needs an external pull-up resistor.

operation.topic: Analog or digital pins and slew rate
operation.text: Any analog-capable pin can be set analog or digital: setting its ANCON0 or ANCON1 bit makes it analog, clearing it makes it digital. Each port's output edge rate can be standard or reduced (the reduced setting gives transitions about a tenth as fast) to cut EMI; reduced is the default for every port. SLRCON holds one bit per port (SLRA-SLRG); SLRF and SLRG are absent on 28, 40 and 44-pin devices and SLRC-SLRE on 28-pin devices.

Seven bits wide (TRISA, LATA). RA5 and RA3:RA0 share the A/D inputs, selected through the ANSELx bits; TRISA still sets their direction and must stay set (input) while they are analog. These pins are analog inputs after any Reset and read 0. RA6 and RA7 serve the primary oscillator (HS modes) or the external clock in and out (EC modes) and are then not digital I/O, their TRIS and LAT bits reading 0; when the default oscillator is one of the internal ones (HF-INTOSC, MF-INTOSC, LF-INTOSC) they turn into digital I/O. RA5 can also be the Timer1 clock input or the Timer3 external gate input.

Eight bits wide (TRISB, LATB). Clearing RBPU (INTCON2<7>) turns on weak pull-ups on all PORTB pins; a pin's pull-up turns off when it is an output, and all are off after a Power-on Reset. RB7:RB4 have interrupt-on-change, on input pins only: the inputs are compared with the value latched at the last PORTB read and any mismatch sets RBIF. To clear it, read or write PORTB (not with MOVFF (ANY), PORTB), wait one instruction cycle, then clear RBIF; while the mismatch lasts RBIF keeps setting. The feature suits wake-on-key-press and uses where PORTB serves only for the change interrupt; polling PORTB while it is in use is discouraged. It can wake the device from power-managed modes. RB3:RB2 are CTMU edge inputs; RB5 can be the Timer3 clock input or the Timer1 external gate input.

Eight bits wide (TRISC, LATC), with Schmitt trigger inputs; RC2 through RC7 are digital only. PORTC carries CCP, MSSP and EUSART functions; the CCP, SPI and EUSART pins can be made open-drain while active (SSPOD, CCPxOD, U1OD in ODCON), and RC1 too when CCP2 is on it (CCP2OD, ODCON<3>). The pins are digital inputs after any Reset. Some peripherals override TRIS to force a pin to output or input; reading TRISC always returns the register contents, not the override.

On 40/44-pin and 64-pin devices only. Eight bits (TRISD, LATD), Schmitt trigger inputs, each pin set separately, digital inputs after any Reset. Weak pull-ups on all pins under RDPU (PADCFG1<7>), off on an output pin and off after every Reset. PORTD can become the 8-bit parallel slave port (PSPMODE, PSPCON<4>), with ST input buffers. RD3 has a CTMU function.

Not on 28-pin devices. Seven bits (TRISE, LATE), Schmitt trigger inputs, each pin set separately, digital inputs after any Reset. Weak pull-ups under REPU (PADCFG1<6>), off on an output pin and after any Reset. RE0, RE1 and RE2 carry the parallel slave port RD, WR and CS controls.

On 64-pin devices only. Eight bits (TRISF, LATF), Schmitt trigger inputs, each pin set separately. RF7:RF1 are analog inputs after a Reset and read 0. Weak pull-ups under RFPU (PADCFG1<5>), off on an output pin and after any Reset.

On 64-pin devices only. Five bits (TRISG, LATG) shared with EUSART, CCP, ECCP, analog, comparator and timer inputs; Schmitt trigger inputs as I/O; EUSART open-drain set through ODCON. Weak pull-ups under RGPU (PADCFG1<4>), off on an output pin and after any Reset. Peripherals may override TRIS, but the override is not written into TRISG, so read-modify-write of TRISG is safe.

On 40/44-pin and 64-pin devices only. With PSPMODE (PSPCON<4>) set, PORTD becomes an 8-bit port that an outside microprocessor reads and writes asynchronously, with RE0 as RD, RE1 as WR and RE2 as CS; TRISE<2:0> must be 111. A write starts when CS and WR are both seen low and ends when either goes high, then PSPIF (PIR1<7>) and IBF (PSPCON<7>) set. A read starts when CS and RD are both low: PORTD data goes out and OBF (PSPCON<6>) sets; when CS or RD goes high the pins return to inputs and PSPIF sets. Firmware waits for PSPIF and then checks IBF and OBF. IBOV flags a write that arrived before the previous word was read; it is cleared in software.

On 64-pin devices only. The DSM ANDs a modulator (data) signal with a carrier and sends the result to MDOUT. The carrier has two parts: while the modulator is high the carrier high (CARH) source is used, while it is low the carrier low (CARL) source. Carriers and modulator come from on-chip peripherals or from pins. This gives frequency-shift, phase-shift and on-off keying. Extras: carrier synchronization, carrier polarity, carrier pin disable, a programmable modulator bit, modulator pin disable, output polarity and slew rate control.

MDEN (MDCON) turns the module on. Clearing it switches both carriers to VSS and the modulator to MDBIT, the lowest-current state; the source selections in the MDSRC, MDCARH and MDCARL registers are kept and apply again when MDEN is set. Clearing MDOE keeps the module mixing but holds MDOUT low. Modulator sources: ECCP1, CCP2-CCP5, MSSP SDO (SPI only), EUSART1 TX1, EUSART2 TX2, the MDMIN pin (RF0) and MDBIT. Carrier sources, chosen with MDCH<3:0> and MDCL<3:0>: CCP1-CCP4, the reference clock, the MDCIN1 (RF2) and MDCIN2 (RF4) pins and VSS.

Switching between carriers can cut a carrier pulse short. With synchronization on, the carrier pulse in progress at the modulator transition is allowed to finish (go low) before the other carrier takes over. MDCHSYNC (MDCARH) enables it for the carrier high side and MDCLSYNC (MDCARL) for the carrier low side; with both on, the modulator edges are aligned to the carrier falling edges.

operation.topic: DSM polarity, pin control, Sleep and Reset
operation.text: MDCHPOL and MDCLPOL invert the carrier high and low sources, and MDOPOL inverts MDOUT. A peripheral chosen as carrier normally also drives its own pin; MDCHODIS and MDCLODIS break that link, and MDSODIS does the same for the modulator source. MDBIT can be the modulator, so firmware sets the data directly. For modulated streams of 20 MHz or more, clear MDSLR to remove the pin's slew rate limit. Sleep does not stop the DSM; it keeps working if its sources still run. Any Reset disables it and returns its registers to their defaults.

Timer or counter, 8-bit or 16-bit, chosen in software; readable and writable; a dedicated 8-bit programmable prescaler; internal or external clock with edge select; interrupt on overflow. T0CON controls it: TMR0ON, T08BIT, T0CS (1 = T0CKI pin, 0 = internal instruction clock), T0SE (1 = increment on the falling edge of T0CKI, 0 = rising), PSA (1 = no prescaler) and T0PS<2:0> (000 = 1:2 up to 111 = 1:256). T0CON resets to all ones: Timer0 on, 8-bit, clocked from T0CKI at the largest prescale.

As a timer (T0CS = 0) it counts every instruction cycle unless a prescaler is assigned; a write to TMR0 stops counting for the next two instruction cycles, which can be allowed for in the value written. As a counter (T0CS = 1) it counts every rising or falling edge on T0CKI, chosen by T0SE. An external clock must meet the requirements for being synchronized to the internal phase clock (TOSC), and counting starts a little after synchronization. In 16-bit mode TMR0H is a buffer: reading TMR0L copies the true high byte into TMR0H, and writing TMR0L loads the high byte from TMR0H, so all 16 bits are read or written at once.

The prescaler is an 8-bit counter that cannot be read or written. PSA = 0 assigns it to Timer0, giving 1:2 to 1:256 in powers of two. Any write to TMR0 (CLRF, MOVWF, BSF and the like) clears the prescaler count but not its assignment, and the assignment can be changed while running. Overflow sets TMR0IF, masked by TMR0IE (INTCON<5>); clear the flag in the handler. Timer0 stops in Sleep, so it cannot wake the device.

A 16-bit timer or counter with readable and writable TMR1H and TMR1L, clocked from the instruction clock, the system clock, the T1CKI pin or the secondary oscillator (with low-power, high-power and external digital clock options). It interrupts on overflow, can be reset by the ECCP special event trigger and has a gate. T1CON holds the clock select (TMR1CS<1:0>), prescale (T1CKPS<1:0>: 1:1, 1:2, 1:4, 1:8), SOSCEN, T1SYNC, RD16 and TMR1ON. Do not use the FOSC clock source with ECCP capture or compare; pick another clock option. With SOSCEN = 0 the SOSC inverter and feedback resistor are off and draw no power.

TMR1ON (T1CON) and TMR1GE (T1GCON) enable it. On an internal clock it counts multiples of FOSC set by the prescaler; on an external clock it counts rising edges of T1CKI and can be synchronized to the system clock or run asynchronously; a 32.768 kHz crystal on the dedicated oscillator can serve as the timer clock. With the SOSC in crystal mode, RC1/SOSCI and RC0/SOSCO/SCLKI become inputs, TRISC<1:0> is ignored and the pins read 0. As a counter it must see a falling edge before the first counting rising edge after Timer1 is enabled after POR, after a write to TMR1H or TMR1L, after Timer1 is disabled, or when Timer1 is enabled while T1CKI is low.
The T1CKI input uses a high-speed Schmitt trigger buffer. The synchronizer does not work in Sleep. The SOSC output depends on the SOSCSEL<1:0> configuration bits.

With RD16 (T1CON<1>) set, TMR1H becomes a buffer for the high byte: reading TMR1L loads it with the true high byte, and writing TMR1L transfers TMR1H into the high byte, so the 16 bits move together and a rollover between byte reads cannot corrupt the value. Writing TMR1H does not clear the prescaler; writing TMR1L does.

A crystal oscillator between SOSCI (input) and SOSCO (amplifier output), low power and rated for 32 kHz crystals. It starts when SOSCEN is set in T1CON or T3CON, when SOSCGO (OSCCON2<3>) is set, or when SCS<1:0> (OSCCON<1:0>) = 01 selects it as the system clock; SOSCGO warms it up before a peripheral asks for it. It keeps running in every power-managed mode. Firmware must wait for it to start. SOSCSEL<1:0> (CONFIG1L<4:3>) sets the drive: 11 is the higher level for a wide range of 32.768 kHz crystals and load ratings; the lower level is tuned for very low power, does not suit every crystal and works only with about 3 pF to 10 pF on each pin. A crystal's CL rating is related to, but not the same as, the C1 and C2 values; test the circuit thoroughly once values are chosen.

operation.topic: SOSC as clock source and layout
operation.text: SCS<1:0> = 01 runs CPU and peripherals from the SOSC (SEC_RUN); with IDLEN clear a SLEEP instruction enters SEC_IDLE. SOSCRUN (OSCCON2<6>) is set while the SOSC supplies the clock, which also tells which source the fail-safe clock monitor left running. The oscillator draws very little power and is sensitive to nearby fast-changing signals, most of all with SOSCSEL<1:0> = 01. Keep it close to the device with no circuits other than VSS or VDD inside its boundary; a grounded guard ring helps when a fast circuit (an ECCP1 pin in compare or PWM, or the primary oscillator on OSC2) must be near. In the low drive mode keep RC2 signals away: either leave RC2 unconnected or make it an input fed by a slow-edged source; if it must be a toggling output, the higher drive mode may be needed. Clean flux residue: its leakage can swamp the oscillator. Timer1 overflow (FFFFh to 0000h) sets TMR1IF (PIR1<0>), enabled by TMR1IE (PIE1<0>).

An ECCP set to compare mode with the special event trigger (CCP1M<3:0> = 1011) and using Timer1 resets it and, if the A/D is enabled, starts a conversion; CCPR1H:CCPR1L then acts as Timer1's period register. Timer1 must run as a timer or synchronous counter; in asynchronous counter mode the reset may fail. A write to Timer1 at the same moment wins. The trigger clears TMR1 but does not set TMR1IF. Which timer each CCP/ECCP uses is set in CCPTMRS.

TMR1GE (T1GCON) enables gate control and T1GPOL (T1GCON<6>) its polarity. With the gate enabled Timer1 counts on rising edges of its clock while the gate is active and holds its count otherwise. T1GSS<1:0> (T1GCON<1:0>) picks the gate source: the T1G pin, the TMR2-to-PR2 match, or the comparator 1 or 2 output (CMP1OUT, CMSTAT<6>; CMP2OUT, CMSTAT<7>), each with selectable polarity. The TMR2 match source is a one-instruction-cycle high pulse each time TMR2 resets after matching PR2: with T1GPOL = 1 Timer1 counts for one cycle after each match, with T1GPOL = 0 it counts all the time except the cycle after the match.

operation.topic: Timer1 gate toggle and single pulse modes
operation.text: Toggle mode (T1GTM, T1GCON<5>) routes the gate via a flip-flop toggling at each incrementing edge, so Timer1 measures a whole gate period rather than one level; clearing T1GTM clears and holds the flip-flop, so the measured edge is known. Single pulse mode (T1GSPM, T1GCON<4>, then T1GGO/T1DONE, T1GCON<3>) enables counting at the next incrementing edge and clears T1GGO/T1DONE on the trailing edge of the pulse; no further gate events count until firmware sets it again, and clearing T1GSPM also clears it. Both modes together measure the gate signal's cycle time. T1GVAL (T1GCON<2>) shows the present gate level, valid even with the gate disabled.

An 8-bit timer (TMR2) with an 8-bit period register (PR2), both readable and writable, counting FOSC/4 through a prescaler of 1:1, 1:4 or 1:16 (T2CKPS<1:0>). Each clock TMR2 is compared with PR2; on a match TMR2 resets to 00h on the next cycle and the match drives a 1:1 to 1:16 postscaler (T2OUTPS<3:0>). TMR2ON (T2CON<2>) turns it off to save power. TMR2 clears on any Reset and PR2 resets to FFh. Prescaler and postscaler counts clear on a write to TMR2, a write to T2CON, and any device Reset (POR, MCLR, WDT or BOR); writing T2CON does not clear TMR2.
The postscaler output sets TMR2IF (PIR1<1>), enabled by TMR2IE (PIE1<1>). The unscaled match output is the PWM time base for the ECCP and CCP modules and can be the MSSP shift clock in SPI mode.

A 16-bit timer or counter like Timer1: readable and writable TMR3H and TMR3L, internal or external clock with system clock and SOSC options, interrupt on overflow, reset by the ECCP special event trigger, gate control. Modes: timer, synchronous counter, asynchronous counter and gated timer. TMR3CS<1:0> = 00 counts FOSC/4, 01 counts FOSC, and 10 counts the SOSC or the T3CKI pin (rising edges, once a falling edge has been seen); prescale 1:1 to 1:8 (T3CKPS<1:0>). Do not use the FOSC source with ECCP capture or compare. T3SYNC is not usable when the device clock comes from Timer1 or Timer3.

RD16 (T3CON<1>) makes TMR3H a buffer so the full 16 bits are read and written together; writing TMR3H does not clear the prescaler, writing TMR3L does. The SOSC can clock Timer3: start it with SOSCEN in T1CON or T3CON, SOSCGO (OSCCON2<3>) or SCS<1:0> = 01, and set TMR3CSx; Timer3 then counts each rising edge of the oscillator.

The same scheme as Timer1: TMR3GE (T3GCON<7>) and T3GPOL (T3GCON<6>); T3GSS<1:0> chooses the T3G pin, the TMR4-to-PR4 match pulse, or comparator 1 or 2 output. Toggle mode (T3GTM, T3GCON<5>), single pulse mode (T3GSPM, T3GCON<4>, with T3GGO/T3DONE, T3GCON<3>) and T3GVAL (T3GCON<2>) work as on Timer1. The falling edge of T3GVAL sets TMR3GIF (PIR2), an interrupt if TMR3GIE (PIE2) is set; the flag works even with the gate disabled.

operation.topic: Timer3 interrupt and special event reset
operation.text: Overflow (FFFFh to 0000h) sets TMR3IF, enabled by TMR3IE. An ECCP using Timer3 in special event trigger compare mode (CCP3M<3:0> = 1011) resets Timer3 and starts an A/D conversion if the A/D is on, making CCPR3H:CCPR3L the period register. Timer3 must be a timer or synchronous counter; asynchronously the reset may fail. A coincident write wins, and the trigger clears TMR3 without setting TMR3IF (PIR2<1>).

An 8-bit timer (TMR4) with an 8-bit period register (PR4), all registers readable and writable, prescaler 1:1, 1:4 or 1:16 (T4CKPS<1:0>: 00 = 1, 01 = 4, 1x = 16) on FOSC/4, postscaler 1:1 to 1:16 (T4OUTPS<3:0>), interrupt on TMR4 matching PR4 (TMR4IF, enabled by TMR4IE). TMR4ON (T4CON<2>) turns it off. TMR4 clears on any Reset; PR4 resets to FFh. Prescaler and postscaler clear on a write to TMR4 or T4CON and on any Reset; writing T4CON does not clear TMR4. Its unscaled output serves only as the ECCP PWM time base, never as an MSSP baud clock.

The charge time measurement unit is an analog module that measures time differences between pulse sources and generates pulses independent of the system clock. With the other analog modules it measures time, capacitance and changes in capacitance, or produces a pulse after a set delay; it suits capacitive sensors. Features: up to 11 channels for capacitance or time (depending on the A/D channels the device has), temperature measurement through an on-chip diode, a precision current source, four edge trigger sources with polarity control, edge sequence and response control, 1 ns time resolution, and delay of an external or internal signal asynchronous to the system clock. It works through the A/D; for time delay it uses a comparator. Edge sources: two external inputs or the ECCP1 and CCP2 special event triggers. The CTMU can trigger the A/D.

A fixed current charges a circuit. For capacitance, current and charging time are fixed and the A/D voltage gives C. For time, current and capacitance are fixed and the voltage gives the time between start and stop. For a delay, current, capacitance and comparator voltage are fixed and the delay is the time to charge to the comparator threshold.

Three current ranges spanning two decades, chosen by IRNG<1:0> (CTMUICON<1:0>), 01 being the lowest. ITRIM<5:0> (CTMUICON<7:2>) trims it in steps of about 2%: 000000 is no change, 011111 the largest increase (about +62%) and 100001 the largest decrease (about -62%).

Edge 1 and Edge 2 each take CTED1, CTED2 or the ECCP1 or CCP2 special event trigger (EDG1SEL, EDG2SEL in CTMUCONL) with polarity set by EDG1POL and EDG2POL (CTMUCONL<4,7>). The inputs respond to level, not transitions. EDGSEQEN (CTMUCONH<2>) requires Edge 1 before Edge 2. EDG1STAT and EDG2STAT (CTMUCONL<1:0>) set when their edge responds, or immediately if a configuration change matches the present level. Current flows to the outside only while exactly one status bit is set; both set or both clear stop it, so it flows only between the edges. Clear both bits, at the same time if possible, before the next measurement. Firmware may set them: one bit set turns the current on, both set or cleared turn it off.

CTMUIF (PIR3<3>) sets each time the current source turns on and then off; CTMUIE (PIE3<3>) enables the interrupt. Without edge sequencing, read the status bits to see which edge came last. Set-up order: IRNG range; ITRIM trim; EDG1SEL and EDG2SEL sources; EDG1POL and EDG2POL polarity (default negative, high to low); EDGSEQEN if wanted (off by default); TGEN (CTMUCONH<4>) for measurement or time delay (default measurement); CTTRIG (CTMUCONH<0>) to start an A/D conversion after the second edge (off by default); set IDISSEN (CTMUCONH<1>) to discharge the circuit, wait, clear it; clear CTMUEN (CTMUCONH<7>); clear EDG2STAT and EDG1STAT together; set EDGEN (CTMUCONH<3>); set CTMUEN. The A/D handles capacitance and time measurement; pulse generation uses comparator 2 and its reference.

Relative measurements, such as a touch key where a finger adds to a baseline capacitance, usually need no calibration. Absolute capacitance or time needs the current source calibrated and the circuit's own capacitance measured or cancelled. The current is within about +/-62% of nominal on each range. To calibrate it: set up the A/D and CTMU, set EDG1STAT, wait for the voltage across RCAL and the sample capacitor to settle, convert, and compute I = V / RCAL. The trim bits can then be adjusted step by step, or the untrimmed value stored for later measurements. Aim the reading at about 70% of full scale, well above the noise; RCAL should be as precise as the measurement needs, 0.1% at least.

The A/D sample capacitor and board strays add to any measured capacitance. With the capacitance under test removed: set up the A/D and CTMU, set EDG1STAT, wait a fixed time t, clear EDG1STAT, convert, and compute COFFSET = (I x t)/V. CAD is about 4 pF. The charging time may need adjusting until the reading is reasonable.

Absolute: calibrate current and offset, set EDG1STAT, wait a fixed T, clear EDG1STAT, convert, compute CTOTAL = (I x T)/V and subtract COFFSET. Relative, for touch keys: set EDG1STAT, wait, clear it and convert; a touch adds body capacitance and lowers the reading, so the voltage itself shows the change and no calibration is needed.

After calibration: set up the A/D and CTMU, set EDG1STAT, then EDG2STAT (or let the edges do it), convert, and compute T = (C/I) x V. CAD + CEXT must leave the voltage in the A/D's range. For the shortest times select an unused channel whose pin has no trace, keeping the total near the A/D's own capacitance (25 pF); for longer times connect an external capacitor to an A/D channel and select it.

A diode's forward voltage at constant current falls as temperature rises, so the CTMU current into a diode and an A/D reading of VF give temperature. A temperature sense diode sits on A/D channel 29; an ordinary junction diode on an A/D pin also works, the A/D multiplexer being shared by CTMU and A/D. The A/D result falls as temperature rises. The diode is neither calibrated nor standardized; calibrate it in the application.

With TGEN set the CTMU produces a pulse on CTPLS independent of the system clock, after a delay set either by an external voltage on CTDIN or by an external capacitor (CDELAY) charged to the comparator 2 trip point set by the comparator voltage reference. CTMUDS (PADCFG1<0>) = 0 uses comparator 2, 1 uses CTDIN. Steps: if CTMUDS is clear set up comparator 2 and the comparator reference; set up the CTMU with TGEN set; set EDG1STAT. A capacitive sensor as CDELAY (a humidity sensor, for one) varies the pulse width; CTDIN suits a digital sensor; CTPLS can feed a capture input to measure the width.

operation.topic: CTMU in Sleep, Idle and Reset
operation.text: Sleep always turns the current source off, so a measurement in progress may end wrongly. In Idle, CTMUSIDL (CTMUCONH<5>) = 0 keeps the module working; 1 turns the current source off, with the same effect as Sleep. A Reset clears every CTMU register, turning the module and its current off; a measurement in progress is lost, and the partial charge on the circuit should be drained (set and clear IDISSEN with the A/D on that channel) before measuring again.

Four capture/compare/PWM modules, CCP2 to CCP5, each with a 16-bit register usable as a capture register, a compare register or a PWM duty register (master and slave). CCPxM<3:0> (CCPxCON) selects: 0000 off (module reset); 0010 compare, toggle on match; 0100 capture every falling edge; 0101 every rising edge; 0110 every 4th rising edge; 0111 every 16th rising edge; 1000 compare, pin starts low and goes high on match; 1001 starts high and goes low; 1010 compare, software interrupt only; 1011 compare, special event trigger (resets the timer, does not start an A/D conversion); 11xx PWM. On CCP2 the capture modes can count received CAN messages instead (CANCAP, CIOCON<4>). DCxB<1:0> are the two low bits of the 10-bit PWM duty; the upper eight are in CCPRxL.

Each module has a control register (CCPxCON) and a 16-bit data register (CCPRxL, CCPRxH), all readable and writable. Capture and compare use Timer1 or Timer3, PWM uses Timer2 or Timer4, chosen per module in CCPTMRS. All modules can run at once and share a timer when in the same kind of mode. In compare or PWM the CCPx output can be open-drain (CCPxOD, ODCON<6:2>), so an external pull-up can take it to a higher voltage without a level shifter.

On an event at the CCPx pin, CCPRxH:CCPRxL captures the 16-bit value of the timer chosen in CCPTMRS. Events: every falling edge, every rising edge, every 4th or every 16th rising edge (CCPxM<3:0>). A capture sets CCPxIF, cleared in software; a second capture before CCPRx is read overwrites the first. The pin must be an input (TRIS set). Timer1 or Timer3 must run as a timer or synchronous counter; in asynchronous counter mode capture may fail. For CCP2 the CAN module can supply the capture trigger instead of the pin, to time-stamp received messages.

Changing the capture mode can raise a false interrupt: keep CCPxIE clear and clear CCPxIF after the change. The prescaler counter clears when the module is off or out of capture mode, so any Reset clears it; changing from one prescale to another does not clear it and may interrupt, so turn the module off (CLRF CCPxCON) and then load the new mode. With CANCAP (CIOCON<4>) set, CCP2 captures when a message lands in any receive buffer, on every message (0100 or 0101), every 4th (0110) or every 16th (0111), in place of events on RC2/CCP2.

CCPRx is compared continuously with the timer pair chosen in CCPTMRS. On a match the pin goes high, goes low, toggles or stays as the I/O latch has it, per CCPxM<3:0>, and CCPxIF sets. The pin must be an output (TRIS clear). Clearing CCPxCON forces the compare output latch low, not the port latch. Timer1 or Timer3 must run as a timer or synchronous counter. Software interrupt mode (1010) leaves the pin alone and only interrupts. Special event trigger mode (1011) resets the module's timer, making CCPRx a programmable period register. The compare interrupt comes as the timer steps from the CCPRx value to the next.

The CCPx pin gives a PWM output of up to 10 bits; its TRIS bit must be clear. The period is set by PR2. When TMR2 equals PR2, on the next increment TMR2 clears, the pin sets (not at 0% duty) and the duty value moves from CCPRxL into CCPRxH. The Timer2 postscaler does not affect the PWM frequency but can set a separate update rate, for a servo for example. Clearing CCPxCON forces the output latch low.

The duty is the 10-bit value CCPRxL:CCPxCON<5:4>, eight high bits in CCPRxL. It can be written any time but loads into CCPRxH (read-only in PWM) only at the next PR2 match, which with a 2-bit internal latch double-buffers it for glitch-free output. The pin clears when CCPRxH and the latch match TMR2 joined to the 2-bit Q clock or prescaler bits. A duty longer than the period never clears the pin. Set-up: write PR2; write CCPRxL and CCPxCON<5:4>; clear the pin's TRIS bit; set the TMR2 prescale and turn Timer2 on in T2CON; put the module in PWM mode.

One enhanced CCP module, ECCP1, controlled by CCP1CON: a standard CCP (16-bit capture, compare or PWM duty register) with an enhanced PWM giving two or four outputs, output steering, programmable polarity, programmable dead band and automatic shutdown and restart. CCP2CON to CCP5CON belong to CCP2 to CCP5.

Two more registers serve the enhanced PWM: ECCP1DEL (dead band, restart) and PSTR1CON (pulse steering); ECCP1AS controls auto-shutdown. Outputs ECCP1/P1A, P1B, P1C and P1D, one, two or four in use depending on P1M<1:0> and CCP1M<3:0>; their TRIS bits must make them outputs. Capture and compare use Timer1 or Timer3, PWM Timer2 or Timer4, chosen in CCPTMRS; capture is meant for a timer in synchronous counter mode and may misbehave asynchronously. Capture stores TMR1 or TMR3 in CCPR1H:CCPR1L on every falling edge, every rising edge, every 4th or every 16th rising edge, sets CCP1IF (PIR3<1>) and overwrites an unread value. The ECCP1 pin must be an input; if it is an output a port write can trigger a capture.

The capture timer must run as a timer or synchronous counter. A mode change can cause a false interrupt; keep CCP1IE clear and clear CCP1IF afterwards. The prescaler clears when the module is off or out of capture mode, but not on a change of prescale, so clear CCP1CON before loading a new mode.

CCPR1 is compared with the timer pair chosen in CCPTMRS; on a match the ECCP1 pin goes high, low, toggles or follows the latch, and CCP1IF sets. The pin must be an output, and the timer must run as a timer or synchronous counter; asynchronously compare does not work reliably. Clearing CCP1CON forces the compare output latch low. Software interrupt mode (1010) only sets CCP1IF. Special event trigger mode (1011) resets the assigned timer, making CCPR1 a period register, and starts an A/D conversion if the A/D is already enabled.

PWM on up to four pins with up to 10-bit resolution, in single, half-bridge, full-bridge forward and full-bridge reverse output modes set by P1M (CCP1CON). Pin polarity is set by the CCP1M bits. On first enabling, the module waits for the start of a new period so it never outputs a partial waveform. Pins not used by the selected mode stay free for other functions.

P1A carries the PWM signal and P1B its complement, for push-pull loads or for a full bridge with four switches driven by two signals. P1DC<6:0> (ECCP1DEL) sets a dead band, in instruction cycles, before each output goes active, to prevent shoot-through; a delay longer than the duty keeps that output inactive for the whole cycle. P1A and P1B TRIS bits must be clear.
All four pins are outputs (TRIS bits clear). Forward: P1A held active, P1D modulated, P1B and P1C inactive. Reverse: P1C held active, P1B modulated, P1A and P1D inactive.

P1M1 (CCP1CON) sets direction; a change takes effect on the next PWM cycle. Before the current period ends the modulated outputs (P1B, P1D) go inactive, the unmodulated ones (P1A, P1C) swap, and modulation resumes at the start of the next period; P1A and P1C switch (1/FOSC) x TMR2 prescale before the end of the current cycle. There is no dead band in full-bridge mode; one is needed only when direction changes at or near 100% duty and the switches turn off slower than they turn on, when shoot-through flows for TOFF - TON. Remedies: lower the duty for one period before reversing, or use drivers that turn the switches off faster than on.

After Reset every I/O pin is high-impedance, so external pull-up or pull-down resistors must hold the power switches off until the PWM drives them. CCP1M<1:0> set active-high or active-low for each pin pair (P1A/P1C, P1B/P1D); choose polarity before enabling the output drivers, as changing it with drivers on can damage the circuit. The output latches may be in the wrong state at initialization: enable the mode, let one full PWM cycle complete (TMR2IF or TMR4IF set as the second period starts), then enable the pin drivers.

An external event can force the PWM pins to a set state. ECCP1AS<2:0> (ECCP1AS<6:4>) choose the sources: 001 C1OUT high, 010 C2OUT high, 011 either, 100 VIL on FLT0, 101 FLT0 or C1OUT, 110 FLT0 or C2OUT, 111 FLT0 or either comparator; 000 disables. Firmware can also set ECCP1ASE. On shutdown ECCP1ASE (ECCP1AS<7>) sets and stays set until firmware clears it or auto-restart does, and the enabled pins go at once to the states chosen per pair by PSS1AC<1:0> and PSS1BD<1:0>: 00 drive 0, 01 drive 1, 1x tri-state. Shutdown follows the level, not an edge, and lasts while the level is present; ECCP1ASE cannot be written meanwhile. After the cause is gone and the PWM restarts, output resumes at the start of the next period.

With P1RSEN (ECCP1DEL<7>) set, ECCP1ASE stays set while the shutdown condition lasts and clears in hardware when it ends; the output returns at the next period, which suits current-mode PWM control. With P1RSEN clear, firmware clears ECCP1ASE to restart.

In a half bridge with both switches modulated, the switches usually turn off slower than they turn on, so switching both at once can short the supply through them. In half-bridge mode a programmable delay holds off each inactive-to-active transition; ECCP1DEL<6:0> set it in instruction cycles (TCY, 4 TOSC).

In single output mode (CCP1M<3:2> = 11, P1M<1:0> = 00) the STR<D:A> bits (PSTR1CON<3:0>) put the PWM signal on any of P1A-P1D, one to four at once; the pins' TRIS bits must be clear. CCP1M<1:0> then set the polarity of P1<D:A>. Auto-shutdown applies, affecting only pins with PWM enabled.
