STRSYNC (PSTR1CON) = 0 steers at the end of the instruction writing PSTR1CON, which can leave a partial PWM pulse but removes the signal at once; STRSYNC = 1 steers at the start of the next PWM period, always giving whole pulses.

operation.topic: ECCP in power-managed modes and Reset
operation.text: In Sleep all clocks stop: Timer2/4 do not count, the module holds its state and a driven ECCP1 pin keeps its level; operation continues on wake-up, though with two-speed start-up the initial HF-INTOSC and postscaler frequency may not be stable at once. In PRI_IDLE the primary clock keeps running the module. If the fail-safe clock monitor sees a clock failure, the device drops to RC_RUN, sets OSCFIF (PIR2) and the ECCP runs from the internal oscillator, possibly at another frequency. Any Reset puts all ports in input mode and the ECCP registers in their reset state, compatible with the non-enhanced CCP of other PIC18 and PIC16 devices.

The Master Synchronous Serial Port is a serial interface for talking to peripherals such as serial EEPROMs, shift registers, display drivers and A/D converters, or to other microcontrollers. It runs either as SPI or as I2C. In I2C it handles master, multi-master and slave modes in hardware, with general call, 7-bit and 10-bit addressing, and 5-bit or 7-bit address masking in slave mode. Its registers are SSPSTAT, SSPCON1 and SSPCON2, whose bits mean different things in SPI and I2C.

SPI moves 8 bits out and 8 bits in at the same time and supports all four SPI modes. It uses SDO on RC5, SDI on RC4 (shared with SDA) and SCK on RC3 (shared with SCL and REFO); in slave mode SS on RA5 can be used as well.

SPI uses SSPCON1 (read/write), SSPSTAT (upper two bits read/write, lower six read-only), the buffer SSPBUF and the shift register SSPSR, which cannot be addressed. On receive SSPSR and SSPBUF form a double buffer: a complete byte moves into SSPBUF and sets SSPIF. On transmit there is no double buffer; writing SSPBUF loads SSPSR as well. SMP chooses whether master input is sampled in the middle or at the end of the data output time and must be 0 in slave mode; CKE chooses which clock edge transmits; BF shows SSPBUF full.

Set-up chooses master or slave, clock polarity (idle level of SCK), input sample phase, the clock edge that shifts data out, the clock rate (master) and slave select use (slave), through SSPCON1<5:0> and SSPSTAT<7:6>. Data shifts MSb first. When 8 bits have arrived they move to SSPBUF and BF and SSPIF are set, so the next byte can arrive before the last one is read; reading SSPBUF clears BF. A write to SSPBUF while a transfer is under way is ignored and sets WCOL, which firmware must clear.
SSPOD (ODCON<7>) turns the SDO and SCK drivers into open-drain outputs, so an outside pull-up can lift the line to a higher voltage without a level shifter.

SSPEN (SSPCON1<5>) turns the port on and claims SDI, SDO, SCK and SS; to change the mode, clear SSPEN, rewrite the SSPCON registers and set it again. SDI direction is handled by the module; SDO needs TRISC<5> clear; SCK needs TRISC<3> clear as master and set as slave; SS needs TRISA<5> set. Setting a TRIS bit the other way disables that one function.

In a master/slave link the master starts each transfer by sending SCK. Both ends shift out on their chosen edge and latch on the opposite one and need the same CKP. Either side's data may be real or dummy, so a transfer can carry data from master to slave, from slave to master, or both ways.

The master can start a transfer at any time by writing SSPBUF. The SPI clock is FOSC/4 (TCY), FOSC/16 (4 TCY), FOSC/64 (16 TCY) or the Timer2 output divided by 2, giving at most 16 Mbps at 64 MHz. CKP (SSPCON1<4>) sets clock polarity; with CKE set, SDO is valid before the first SCK edge. A receive-only master can turn SDO into an input and keep clocking bytes in, which works as a line activity monitor.

In slave mode data moves as clock pulses arrive on SCK, whose high and low times may not be shorter than the electrical specification allows; SSPIF is set when the last bit is latched. The slave can send and receive while the device sleeps and can wake it when a byte arrives.

With SS control enabled (SSPCON1<3:0> = 0100) a low SS enables transmit and receive and drives SDO; a high SS releases SDO, even in mid-byte, and resets the module, forcing its bit counter to 0 (clearing SSPEN does the same). In slave mode with CKE set, SS control must be enabled. Outside pull-up or pull-down resistors may be wanted on the released line. For two-wire operation SDO can be tied to SDI and switched to an input while receiving; SDI can stay an input since it cannot cause a bus conflict.

operation.topic: SPI in power-managed modes and Reset
operation.text: In master mode the module clock may differ from full-power operation; in Sleep every clock stops and a transfer freezes until wake-up, then carries on. In Idle modes the peripherals still get a clock from the primary, SOSC or INTOSC source. An enabled MSSP interrupt can wake the device from Sleep or Idle when the master finishes a byte. In slave mode the shift register runs from the outside clock, so bytes can be received in any power-managed mode and the interrupt wakes the device after 8 bits. A Reset turns the MSSP off and ends the current transfer.

In I2C mode the MSSP implements every master and slave function of the standard-mode specification, including general call, with interrupts on Start and Stop bits so firmware can tell when the bus is free, and 7-bit or 10-bit addressing. SCL is RC3 and SDA is RC4; both must be set as inputs through their TRIS bits. The registers are SSPCON1, SSPCON2, SSPSTAT, SSPBUF, SSPSR (not addressable), SSPADD and SSPMSK. SSPADD holds the slave address in slave mode and the baud rate reload value in master mode. SSPMSK, the 7-bit masking value, shares its SFR address with SSPADD; it can be reached only through a dedicated SSPM<3:0> setting. Receive is double-buffered; transmit is not.

SSPEN (SSPCON1<5>) enables the module, and SSPCON1<3:0> choose master mode (clock from the BRG), 7-bit slave, 10-bit slave, either slave mode with Start/Stop interrupts, or firmware-controlled master with the slave idle. Any I2C mode with SSPEN set makes SCL and SDA open-drain, provided their TRISC bits are set. Pull-up resistors on SCL and SDA must be fitted outside the device.

In slave mode SCL and SDA are inputs (TRISC<4:3> set) and the module takes over the pin when it has to transmit. An address match always interrupts; with masking one interrupt can cover up to 31 addresses (7-bit) or 63 (10-bit), and Start/Stop interrupts can be chosen as well. On a match, or on a data byte after a match, the hardware sends ACK and copies SSPSR into SSPBUF. No ACK is sent if BF or SSPOV was already set when the byte came in; SSPIF is still set, SSPBUF is not loaded, reading SSPBUF clears BF and SSPOV is cleared by firmware. Timing parameters 100 and 101 give the shortest SCL high and low times allowed.

After a Start the 8 incoming bits shift into SSPSR on rising SCL edges, and SSPSR<7:1> is compared with SSPADD on the falling edge of the eighth clock. On a match with BF and SSPOV clear, SSPBUF is loaded, BF is set, ACK is sent, and SSPIF goes high as the ninth clock falls. A 10-bit address takes two bytes: the first is 11110 A9 A8 0 with R/W showing a write, and UA is set after each address byte to tell firmware to load SSPADD with the other address byte, which releases SCL. A slave transmitter then sees a Repeated Start and the high address byte again.

A masked address bit is ignored in the comparison, so one masked bit lets two addresses match and more bits let more through; firmware tells which address was used by reading SSPBUF. The MSSPMSK configuration bit chooses 5-bit masking (programmed, 0) or 7-bit masking (unprogrammed, 1, the default). Both work with 7-bit and 10-bit addresses. The two most significant address bits are never masked.

In 5-bit mode the mask sits in ADMSK<5:1> (SSPCON2<5:1>); SSPCON2 then no longer acts as a control register in slave mode. A set ADMSK bit makes the matching SSPADD bit a don't-care, allowing up to 31 addresses with 7-bit and 63 with 10-bit addressing. With 7-bit addresses ADMSK<5:1> mask address bits 5 to 1; with 10-bit addresses ADMSK<5:2> mask bits 5 to 2 and ADMSK1 masks the two low bits together. Example: SSPADD<7:1> = A0h with ADMSK<5:1> = 00111 acknowledges A0h, A2h, A4h, A6h, A8h, AAh, ACh and AEh; in 10-bit mode the same values acknowledge A0h to AFh.

In 7-bit mode the mask is SSPMSK, up to 8 bits, allowing up to 127 addresses with 7-bit and 255 with 10-bit addressing. A clear SSPMSK bit masks the address bit; a set bit demands a match. SSPMSK resets to all ones, so it changes nothing until written. With 7-bit addresses SSPMSK<7:1> apply, with 10-bit SSPMSK<7:0>. To load it, select MSSP mode 1001 (SSPCON1<3:0>), write the mask to the SSPADD address (FC8h), then select the slave mode (0110 for 7-bit, 0111 for 10-bit). Example: SSPADD<7:1> = 1010 000 with SSPMSK<7:1> = 1111 001 acknowledges ACh, A8h, A4h and A0h.

When the address byte matches with R/W clear, SSPSTAT R/W clears, the address goes to SSPBUF and SDA is held low for ACK. With BF or SSPOV set no ACK is given. Each data byte raises an MSSP interrupt; SSPIF is cleared by firmware and SSPSTAT shows the byte's status. With SEN (SSPCON2<0>) set, SCL is held low after each byte until CKP (SSPCON1<4>) is set.

When the address byte matches with R/W set, SSPSTAT R/W sets, the address goes to SSPBUF, ACK is sent on the ninth bit and SCL is held low whatever SEN is, so the master waits while the slave prepares data. Firmware loads SSPBUF (which loads SSPSR) and sets CKP to release SCL; the 8 bits leave on falling SCL edges so SDA is steady while SCL is high. The master's ACK is latched on the ninth rising edge: a NACK (SDA high) ends the transfer and the slave waits for the next Start; an ACK means the next byte must be loaded and CKP set again. SSPIF goes high as the ninth clock falls.

Both slave modes stretch the clock automatically when transmitting; SEN (SSPCON2<0>) adds stretching on receive, holding SCL low at the end of each received byte. In 7-bit receive with SEN set, if BF is set at the falling edge of the ninth clock, CKP clears and holds SCL low until firmware sets it, which prevents overruns; reading SSPBUF before that edge avoids the stretch. In 10-bit receive the address phase stretches whenever UA is set after the ninth clock, without clearing CKP, and SCL is released when SSPADD is updated; stretching on BF happens only in data bytes. In 7-bit transmit CKP clears after the ninth falling edge if BF is clear, whatever SEN is; loading SSPBUF before that edge avoids it. In 10-bit transmit the first two address bytes stretch on UA, and after the third (high address with R/W set) stretching follows BF as in 7-bit transmit. CKP can be set by firmware at any time.

Clearing CKP forces SCL low only once SCL has already been seen low, so it waits for an outside master to pull the line down. After CKP is set, SCL stays low until every other device has released it, so setting CKP cannot shorten the minimum SCL high time.

The general call address, all zeros with R/W = 0, is one of eight addresses the I2C protocol reserves and addresses every device. With GCEN (SSPCON2<7>) set, the incoming byte is compared with both SSPADD and the fixed general call address; on a general call match SSPSR goes to SSPBUF, BF sets on the eighth bit and SSPIF on the falling edge of the ninth. Reading SSPBUF tells a general call from a device address. In 10-bit mode a general call needs no second address byte: UA stays clear and data reception starts after the ACK.

Master mode is chosen with the SSPM bits and SSPEN; the hardware drives SCL and SDA when their TRIS bits are set. Start and Stop detection raise interrupts, and P and S clear on Reset or when the module is turned off. The bus may be taken when P is set or when S and P are both clear. Firmware-controlled master mode leaves all bus actions to code. Once enabled, the master can issue a Start, a Repeated Start, a byte write to SSPBUF (address or data), a receive, an Acknowledge at the end of a received byte, or a Stop. SSPIF is set by a Start, a Stop, a byte sent or received, an Acknowledge sent and a Repeated Start. Events cannot be queued: writing SSPBUF before a Start completes is ignored and sets WCOL.

The master generates all clock pulses as well as Start and Stop; each transfer ends with a Stop or a Repeated Start, and a Repeated Start keeps the bus. As transmitter the first byte is the 7-bit slave address with R/W = 0, followed by data bytes, each answered by an ACK from the slave; as receiver the first byte carries R/W = 1 and the master sends an ACK after each received byte. The baud rate generator sets SCL to 100 kHz, 400 kHz or 1 MHz. A transmit runs: set SEN for a Start; SSPIF sets after the start time; load the address into SSPBUF; the 8 bits shift out; the slave's ACK is written to SSPCON2<6>; SSPIF sets at the end of the ninth clock; load data and repeat; set PEN (SSPCON2<2>) for a Stop, which raises an interrupt when done.

In master mode the BRG reload value is the 8 bits of SSPADD. A write to SSPBUF starts the BRG, which counts down to 0 and stops until reloaded; it counts twice per instruction cycle, on Q2 and Q4, and reloads itself in master mode. When an operation ends (the last data bit followed by ACK) the clock stops and SCL stays where it was. An SSPADD value of 00h is not supported.

Whenever the master releases SCL during a receive, transmit, Repeated Start or Stop, the BRG holds its count until SCL is actually seen high, then reloads from SSPADD<6:0> and counts. SCL high time is therefore at least one BRG rollover even when another device holds the clock low.

Setting SEN (SSPCON2<0>) with SDA and SCL high loads the BRG from SSPADD<6:0>; if both are still high when it times out (TBRG), SDA is pulled low, which is the Start and sets S (SSPSTAT<3>). After another TBRG, SEN clears in hardware and the Start is complete with SDA held low. If SDA and SCL are already low at the beginning, or SCL goes low before SDA is driven low, a bus collision occurs: BCLIF sets, the Start is abandoned and the module returns to idle. Writing SSPBUF during the Start sets WCOL and leaves the buffer unchanged; the lower 5 bits of SSPCON2 cannot be written until the Start is done.

With the module idle, setting RSEN (SSPCON2<1>) pulls SCL low; once SCL is seen low the BRG loads and SDA is released for one TBRG; if SDA is then high, SCL is released, and after SCL is seen high SDA and SCL must stay high for one TBRG before SDA is pulled low for one TBRG with SCL high. RSEN then clears and SDA stays low; S sets when the Start is detected and SSPIF after the BRG times out. The address (7-bit) or first address byte (10-bit) may then be written to SSPBUF. RSEN written during another event does nothing. A collision occurs if SDA is low when SCL rises, or SCL falls before SDA is pulled low. Writing SSPBUF during the sequence sets WCOL; SSPCON2<4:0> cannot be written until it completes.

Writing SSPBUF sets BF, starts the BRG and the next byte. Each bit is put on SDA after SCL falls (hold time, parameter 106) and must be valid before SCL is released (setup time, parameter 107); SCL stays low and then high for one TBRG each. After the eighth falling edge BF clears and the master releases SDA for the slave's ACK, which is sampled at the ninth falling edge into ACKSTAT (SSPCON2<6>): clear for ACK, set for NACK. Then SSPIF sets and the BRG stops, holding SCL low, until SSPBUF is written again. BF is set by the CPU write and cleared when all 8 bits are out. Writing SSPBUF during a transmit sets WCOL; a rewrite within 2 TCY of the first write sets WCOL but updates SSPBUF, which can corrupt the transfer. WCOL must be cleared by firmware.

Setting RCEN (SSPCON2<3>) starts a receive; the module must be inactive first or RCEN is ignored. On each BRG rollover SCL toggles and data shifts into SSPSR. After the eighth falling edge RCEN clears, SSPSR moves to SSPBUF, BF and SSPIF set and the BRG stops with SCL low; reading SSPBUF clears BF. An Acknowledge is then sent by setting ACKEN (SSPCON2<4>). SSPOV sets if a byte completes while BF is still set. Writing SSPBUF while a byte is shifting in sets WCOL and leaves the buffer unchanged.

Setting ACKEN pulls SCL low and puts ACKDT on SDA (clear for ACK, set for NACK). After one TBRG SCL is released; once it is seen high the BRG counts another TBRG and pulls SCL low, then ACKEN clears, the BRG stops and the module goes inactive. Writing SSPBUF during the sequence sets WCOL.

Setting PEN (SSPCON2<2>) at the end of a transfer, with SCL held low after the ninth falling edge, pulls SDA low; once SDA is seen low the BRG counts down, then SCL is released, and one TBRG later SDA is released. When SDA is seen high with SCL high, P (SSPSTAT<4>) sets; a TBRG later PEN clears and SSPIF sets. Writing SSPBUF during the Stop sets WCOL.

In Sleep the I2C module can still receive addresses or data and, with the MSSP interrupt enabled, wake the device on an address match or a completed byte. A Reset turns the module off and ends the current transfer.

Start and Stop interrupts show when the bus is free: P and S clear on Reset or when the module is turned off, the bus may be taken when P is set or both are clear, and with the bus busy an enabled MSSP interrupt fires at the Stop. The hardware watches SDA and reports a mismatch in BCLIF. Arbitration can be lost during address transfer, data transfer, a Start, a Repeated Start or an Acknowledge. A collision happens when the master lets SDA float high for a 1 and another master pulls it to 0: BCLIF sets and the port returns to idle. A transmit in progress stops, BF clears, SDA and SCL are released and SSPBUF can be written; a Start, Repeated Start, Stop or Acknowledge in progress is abandoned and its SSPCON2 control bit cleared. The master keeps watching the bus, SSPIF sets at a Stop, and a write to SSPBUF restarts transmission from the first data bit.

A collision is flagged if SDA or SCL is low when the Start begins, or SCL goes low before SDA is pulled low; the Start is then abandoned, BCLIF sets and the module goes inactive. With SDA seen high the BRG loads from SSPADD<6:0>; SCL seen low while SDA is high counts as a collision (another master sending a 1). If SDA is pulled low by someone else during the count, the BRG resets and SDA is pulled low early without a collision, since two masters cannot start at exactly the same moment and the address that follows is arbitrated; SCL low during the second count is no collision either. At the end of that count SCL is pulled low.

operation.topic: Bus collision during a Repeated Start
operation.text: A collision is flagged if SDA is low when SCL goes from low to high (another master sending a 0), or if SCL goes low before SDA is pulled low (another master sending a 1). After SDA is released the BRG loads from SSPADD<6:0>, SCL is released and, once high, SDA is sampled. If SDA is high the BRG reloads; SDA falling before the time-out is no collision. If both lines are still high at the time-out, SDA is pulled low, the BRG reloads, and at the end of the count SCL is pulled low whatever its state, which completes the Repeated Start.

The Stop begins with SDA low; SCL is released and, once seen high, the BRG loads from SSPADD<6:0> and counts down. A collision is flagged if SDA is low after the BRG times out with SDA released, or if SCL is seen low before SDA goes high; both mean another master is driving a 0.

Every device has two independent EUSARTs, EUSART1 and EUSART2, also called SCI. Each runs as a full-duplex asynchronous port (with wake-up on a received character, automatic baud calibration and 12-bit Break transmit) for terminals or computers, or as a half-duplex synchronous master or slave, with selectable clock polarity, for parts such as A/D or D/A converters and serial EEPROMs. Auto-baud, wake-up on Sync Break and Break transmit suit LIN/J2602 bus systems.

To use the pins as a EUSART, set SPEN (RCSTAx<7>) and the pins' TRIS bits; in asynchronous and synchronous master modes the TRIS bit of the transmit/clock pin is cleared, and in synchronous slave mode it stays set.

Each EUSART has its own 8-bit or 16-bit baud rate generator, 8-bit by default and 16-bit with BRG16 (BAUDCONx<3>). SPBRGHx:SPBRGx fix the period of a timer that runs freely; for asynchronous use BRGH (TXSTAx<2>) and BRG16 also set the rate, and in synchronous mode BRGH is ignored. The nearest integer register value follows from the formula and the error from that integer. BRGH = 1 or the 16-bit generator can cut the error or reach slow rates from a fast oscillator. Writing SPBRGHx:SPBRGx resets the timer, so the new rate starts at once.

operation.topic: EUSART clock in power-managed modes and RX sampling
operation.text: The baud rate comes from the device clock; a power-managed mode may run a clock at another frequency, which may call for a new SPBRGHx:SPBRGx value. The RXx pin is sampled three times and a majority circuit decides high or low.

Automatic baud detection works only in asynchronous mode with WUE clear. Setting ABDEN starts it at the next Start bit: the state machine clears the BRG and the RXx signal times the BRG instead of the other way round. The incoming byte must be 55h (ASCII U, the LIN/J2602 Sync character); measuring across a low bit and a high bit cancels any asymmetry. After the Start bit SPBRGx counts up from the first rising edge, and at the fifth rising edge (the Stop bit) SPBRGHx:SPBRGx hold the bit period and ABDEN clears. During measurement the BRG runs at one eighth of its configured clock; BRG16 must be set to use both registers as a 16-bit counter, and in 8-bit modes SPBRGHx reading 00h shows no carry. A rollover from FFFFh to 0000h sets ABDOVF (BAUDCONx<7>), which firmware can also set or clear; detection keeps running and ABDEN stays set. The EUSART state machine idles during detection, RCxIF sets at the fifth rising edge, and RCREGx must be read to clear it and its content thrown away. With WUE set together with ABDEN, detection takes the byte after the Break. Firmware must check that the incoming rate is reachable from the BRG clock; setting BRG16 widens the range. The transmitter cannot be used during detection: TXREGx cannot be written while ABDEN is set, and ABDEN must not be set during a transmit.

Clearing SYNC (TXSTAx<4>) selects asynchronous mode: NRZ frames (a Start bit, 8 or 9 data bits, a Stop bit), sent LSb first. Transmitter and receiver work independently with the same format and baud rate; the BRG gives a clock at 16 or 64 times the bit rate according to BRGH and BRG16. There is no hardware parity; it can be computed in firmware and sent as the ninth bit. The mode includes the BRG, sampling circuit, transmitter, receiver, wake-up on Sync Break, 12-bit Break transmit and auto-baud.

The transmit shift register TSR is fed from the buffer TXREGx and is reloaded only after the Stop bit of the previous byte has gone. When TXREGx hands its byte to TSR (one TCY) TXxIF sets, whatever TXxIE is; TXxIF cannot be cleared by firmware and becomes valid only in the second instruction cycle after TXREGx is loaded, so polling it at once gives a wrong answer. TRMT (TXSTAx<1>), read-only and without an interrupt, is set when TSR is empty; TSR itself is not in data memory. Setting TXEN sets TXxIF. Set-up: load SPBRGHx:SPBRGx and choose BRGH and BRG16; clear SYNC and set SPEN; set TXxIE for interrupts; set TX9 for 9-bit (address/data marking); set TXEN; put the ninth bit in TX9D; write TXREGx to start; with interrupts, set GIE and PEIE (INTCON<7:6>).

Data from RXx enters a recovery block, a fast shifter running at 16 times the baud rate, while the main receive shifter works at the bit rate or FOSC. Set-up: load the baud rate registers and BRGH/BRG16; clear SYNC and set SPEN; set RCxIE for interrupts; set RX9 for 9-bit data; set CREN to receive. RCxIF sets when a byte is complete. Read RCSTAx for the ninth bit and the error flags, then RCREGx for the data; clearing CREN clears an error. A third byte arriving while two wait unread sets OERR (overrun). With interrupts, GIE and PEIE must be set.

For RS-485 style networks: set the baud rate, clear SYNC and set SPEN, set RX9 and ADDEN, choose the interrupt priority with RCxIP and set CREN. RCxIF sets when a byte is complete and interrupts when RCxIE and GIE are set. Read RCSTAx for errors and the ninth bit and RCREGx to see whether the device is addressed; on an error clear CREN. Once addressed, clearing ADDEN lets every following byte into the buffer and raise an interrupt.

In Sleep the EUSART has no clock, so the BRG stops and a byte cannot be received normally. Setting WUE (BAUDCONx<1>) in asynchronous mode puts the receiver in idle, watching RXx/DTx for a falling edge (the start of a LIN/J2602 Sync Break or wake-up character) whatever the CPU is doing. The edge raises RCxIF, in step with the Q clocks when running and asynchronously in Sleep; reading RCREGx clears it. WUE clears by itself at the next rising edge on RXx, after which the module returns to normal reception. Because wake-up reacts to rising edges, any change before the Stop bit can look like an end of character and give data or framing errors, so the first character must be all zeros: 00h for RS-232 parts, 000h (12 bits) for LIN/J2602. With slow-starting oscillators (HS, HSPLL) the Break must be long enough and followed by enough idle time for the oscillator to start and the EUSART to set up.

The wake-up event sets RCxIF and WUE clears at the following rising edge; the byte then in RCREGx is normally dummy data to discard. Neither WUE nor RCxIF proves the received data is good, so a separate check in firmware is advised. To avoid losing data, check RCIDL to confirm no reception is in progress before setting WUE just before Sleep. If the oscillator takes long to start, WUE can clear before the clock is ready; the sequence should not rely on Q clocks.

For LIN/J2602 the EUSART can send a Break: a Start bit, twelve 0 bits and a Stop bit. It goes out whenever SENDB (TXSTAx<3>) and TXEN (TXSTAx<5>) are set while the shift register is loaded; the byte written to TXREGx only triggers it and is replaced by zeros. SENDB clears in hardware after the Stop bit, so the next byte (usually the Sync character) can be queued behind it. TRMT shows activity as in normal transmission. A LIN master header: configure the mode; set TXEN and SENDB; write a dummy byte to TXREGx; write 55h to TXREGx for the Sync byte; after the Break, SENDB resets and the Sync byte goes out in the set mode; when TXxIF shows TXREGx empty the next byte can be written.

A Break can be received by setting the baud rate to 9/13 of the normal speed, which puts the Stop bit transition at the right sampling point (13 bits of Break against a Start bit and 8 data bits), or with auto-wake-up, which samples the next two transitions on RXx/DTx, raises RCxIF, then receives the next byte with another interrupt. After a Break, auto-baud detect is usually enabled; ABDEN can be set once TXxIF is seen.

SYNC (TXSTAx<4>) selects synchronous mode and CSRC (TXSTAx<7>) master; SPEN (RCSTAx<7>) turns TXx and RXx into the clock line CKx and the data line DTx. Data moves half duplex: receiving is blocked while transmitting and the other way round. The master sends the clock on CKx; TXCKP (BAUDCONx<4>) sets the idle level of CKx high when set and low when clear, which supports Microwire devices.

The transmitter is the same TSR fed from TXREGx, reloaded after the last bit of the previous byte. TXxIF sets when TXREGx passes its byte to TSR (one TCY), whatever TXxIE is, and clears only when TXREGx is loaded again. TRMT shows TSR empty and has no interrupt. Set-up: load SPBRGHx:SPBRGx and choose BRG16; set SYNC, SPEN and CSRC; set TXxIE for interrupts; set TX9 for 9-bit; set TXEN; load TX9D; write TXREGx to start; with interrupts, set GIE and PEIE.

Reception starts with SREN (RCSTAx<5>) for one word or CREN (RCSTAx<4>) for continuous words until CREN is cleared; with both set CREN wins. Data on RXx is sampled on the falling clock edge. Set-up: load the baud rate and BRG16; set SYNC, SPEN and CSRC; make sure CREN and SREN are clear; set RCxIE for interrupts; set RX9 for 9-bit; set SREN or CREN. RCxIF sets when a word is complete; read RCSTAx for the ninth bit and errors, then RCREGx; clear CREN to clear an error; with interrupts, set GIE and PEIE.

Clearing CSRC selects slave mode: the shift clock comes from outside on CKx, so the device can send or receive in any low-power mode. Transmission matches master mode except in Sleep: with two words written to TXREGx before SLEEP, the first moves to TSR and is sent, the second waits in TXREGx without setting TXxIF; when the first has left, the second moves to TSR and TXxIF sets, which wakes the device if TXxIE is set and branches to the interrupt vector if global interrupts are on. Set-up: set SYNC and SPEN, clear CSRC; clear CREN and SREN; set TXxIE for interrupts; set TX9 for 9-bit; set TXEN; load TX9D; write TXREGx; set GIE and PEIE for interrupts.

Reception matches master mode except in Sleep or Idle, and SREN has no effect in slave mode. With CREN set before entering Sleep or Idle, a word can arrive during the low-power mode; RSR then moves it to RCREGx and, with RCxIE set, the interrupt wakes the device (and branches to the vector if global interrupts are on). Set-up: set SYNC and SPEN, clear CSRC; set RCxIE for interrupts; set RX9 for 9-bit; set CREN; RCxIF sets when done; read RCSTAx, then RCREGx; clear CREN on an error; set GIE and PEIE for interrupts.

The A/D converter is a 13-bit differential converter that also gives 12-bit single-ended results, with 8 inputs on 28-pin devices and 11 on 40/44-pin and 64-pin devices. Its registers are ADCON0 (operation), ADCON1 (voltage reference and special trigger), ADCON2 (clock source, programmed acquisition time and justification), ANCON0 and ANCON1 (port configuration), and the result pair ADRESH:ADRESL.

The converter measures the difference between two channels: CHS<4:0> (ADCON0<6:2>) choose the positive input and CHSN<2:0> (ADCON1<2:0>) the negative input, both feeding a unity-gain differential amplifier ahead of the converter. The 12-bit result lands in ADRESH:ADRESL with one more bit giving its sign. Clearing CHSN<2:0> connects the negative input to AVSS inside the device for a single-channel measurement.

ADRESH:ADRESL, 16 bits, receive the 12-bit result and the extended sign bits (ADSGNx) at the end of a conversion; ADFM sets left or right justification. The result is two's complement, so right-justified the pair reads as one signed integer, which eases 16-bit arithmetic. With the converter off, both registers can be used as general purpose registers.

The reference is chosen in firmware: AVDD and AVSS, or the RA3/VREF+/AN3 and RA2/VREF-/AN2 pins; VREF+ can also be an internal 2.0V or 4.1V reference. Each A/D pin can be an analog input or digital I/O; an ANSEL bit set makes the pin analog, turning off its digital input so it reads 0. AN14 to AN11 and AN7 to AN5 exist only on 40/44-pin and 64-pin devices. The converter works by successive approximation on the sample-and-hold output and can run in Sleep if clocked from its own RC oscillator. At the end of a conversion the result goes to ADRESH:ADRESL, GO/DONE (ADCON0<1>) clears and ADIF (PIR1<6>) sets. A device Reset turns the module off and aborts a conversion; ADRESH:ADRESL keep their value through other Resets but hold unknown data after a Power-on Reset.

After configuration the selected channel must be acquired before a conversion starts, with its TRIS bit set as an input; an acquisition time can also be programmed to run between setting GO/DONE and the start of conversion. Steps: set the analog pins (ANCON0, ANCON1), the reference (ADCON1), the positive and negative channels (ADCON0, ADCON1), the acquisition time and conversion clock (ADCON2), and turn the module on (ADCON0); optionally clear ADIF, set ADIE and GIE; wait the acquisition time if needed; set GO/DONE; wait for GO/DONE to clear or for the interrupt; read ADRESH:ADRESL and clear ADIF if needed. TAD is the conversion time per bit, and at least 2 TAD must pass before the next acquisition.

The input path has a pin capacitance CPIN of 5 pF, protection diodes to VDD and VSS (VT = 0.6V), a pin leakage of ±100 nA, an interconnect resistance RIC of 1 kΩ or less, a sampling switch with resistance RSS (falling as VDD rises) and a hold capacitor CHOLD of 25 pF.

For full accuracy CHOLD must charge completely to the channel voltage; the source impedance RS and the switch resistance RSS, which varies with VDD, set the charging time. Leakage through the source impedance offsets the input. The highest source impedance recommended is 2.5 kΩ. After selecting or changing a channel, it must be sampled for at least the minimum acquisition time before conversion. Starting a conversion disconnects the hold capacitor from the pin. The calculation allows a 1/2 LSb error, the most the converter may have and still meet its resolution.

ADCON2 can add an acquisition time each time GO/DONE is set. With ACQT<2:0> (ADCON2<5:3>) at their Reset value 000, setting GO/DONE stops sampling and starts the conversion at once, and firmware must have waited the acquisition time after choosing the channel; this matches devices without programmable acquisition. Other ACQT values keep sampling for the chosen time after GO/DONE is set and then convert, so no wait is needed. Either way, at the end GO/DONE clears, ADIF sets and sampling of the selected channel resumes; with a programmed time nothing shows whether acquisition has ended or conversion has begun.

A 12-bit conversion takes 14 TAD. TAD can be 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64 TOSC or the internal RC oscillator, and must be as short as possible while staying above the minimum TAD of parameter 130 (Table 31-26).

ANCON0, ANCON1 and the TRIS registers control the A/D pins. An analog input needs its TRIS bit set; with the pin set as an output, its digital output level is what gets converted. The A/D works regardless of CHS<3:0> and the TRIS bits. Analog-configured pins read 0 in the PORT register; a pin set as a digital input still converts its analog level accurately, but an analog level on a digital input can make its input buffer draw more current than the specification allows.

With ACQT<2:0> = 000 the conversion starts one instruction after GO/DONE is set, leaving room to enter Sleep first; with ACQT<2:0> = 010 a 4 TAD acquisition comes first. The hold capacitor disconnects about 100 ns into the conversion; on the next Q4 after the last bit ADRESH:ADRESL are loaded, GO/DONE clears, ADIF sets and the capacitor reconnects. Clearing GO/DONE mid-conversion aborts it, leaving ADRESH:ADRESL with the previous result (or the last value written). A 2 TAD wait follows any finished or aborted conversion, after which acquisition of the selected channel starts by itself. GO/DONE must not be set by the same instruction that turns the converter on.

The special event trigger of CCP2 (CCP2M<3:0> = 1011), ECCP1, the CTMU (CTTRIG, CTMUCONH<0>, set) or Timer1 can start a conversion. The module must be on (ADON = 1), the channel chosen and the acquisition time provided, by firmware timing or a TACQ setting; the trigger then sets GO/DONE and acquisition begins. With ADON = 0 the trigger is ignored. An ECCP1 or CCP2 trigger also clears Timer1 or Timer3, which repeats the acquisition period automatically, and the timer still resets when the A/D is off.

ACQT<2:0> and ADCS<2:0> should suit the clock of the power-managed mode in use. A conversion can be started after entering a power-managed Run mode and the device should stay on that clock until it ends; it may enter the matching Idle mode meanwhile. Below 1 MHz the A/D RC clock should be selected. Sleep operation needs the A/D RC clock; with ACQT<2:0> = 000 the conversion waits one instruction cycle so SLEEP can execute, and IDLEN and SCS<1:0> (OSCCON) must already be clear.

The module holds two comparators, each configured on its own. Inputs come from analog pins and two internal references; outputs go to pins and can be read in a register. Each has its own input selection, output polarity and interrupt on a chosen output change. CM1CON and CM2CON set inputs, outputs and interrupts; CMSTAT holds the read-only output bits.

The output is low when VIN+ is below VIN- and high when VIN+ is above it, with an uncertain band from input offset and response time. Response time is the delay after a new reference or input source is selected before the output is valid; it differs from the settling time of the voltage reference, so both count toward the total delay, or the maximum comparator delay from the electrical characteristics can be used.

Analog pins share a digital output, so each carries reverse-biased protection diodes to both rails, so an input must stay between VSS and VDD; going more than 0.6V beyond either rail forward-biases a diode and can cause latch-up. A source impedance of at most 10 kΩ is recommended, and parts on the input such as a capacitor or Zener should leak very little. The input model has CPIN of 5 pF and pin leakage of ±100 nA.

Each comparator has up to eight input combinations from up to four outside inputs and two internal references. The non-inverting input is the CxINA pin (CREF = 0, CMxCON<2>) or CVREF from the comparator voltage reference (CREF = 1). The inverting input, chosen by CCH<1:0> (CMxCON<1:0>), is CxINB, CxINC, C2INB/C1INB or the internal reference VBG (1.024V nominal). Outside references must lie between VSS and VDD and may go on either input. The selected input pin needs both its TRIS bit and its ANSELx bit set.

CON (CMxCON<7>) turns a comparator on; clearing it gives the lowest current. CMSTAT<6> reads comparator 1 and CMSTAT<7> comparator 2 (read-only). COE (CMxCON<6>) puts the output on the RE2 and RE1 pins through the pin multiplexers, with TRISE<2:1> still acting as the output enables. The output is high when VIN+ exceeds VIN-; CPOL (CMxCON<5>) inverts it.

EVPOL<1:0> (CMxCON<4:3>) choose the event: 01 interrupts when the output rises, 10 when it falls, 11 on any change of either comparator (firmware tracks CMSTAT<7:6> to see which), and 00 never sets the flag. CPOL inversion acts like swapping the inputs. The flags CMPxIF (PIR4<5:4>) are cleared by firmware and can be written to 1 to simulate an interrupt. The interrupt needs CMPxIE (PIE4<5:4>), PEIE (INTCON<6>) and GIE (INTCON<7>); the flags still set with any of them clear.

An active comparator keeps working in Sleep and its interrupt, if enabled, wakes the device; each running comparator draws extra current, so turning them off (CON = 0) before Sleep saves power. CMxCON is unchanged by a wake-up. A Reset returns CMxCON to its Reset state, turning off both comparators and the voltage reference.

A 32-tap resistor ladder gives a selectable reference, mainly for the comparators though it can be used on its own. The ladder is segmented to cover a range of CVREF values and can be powered down when unused. CVRSS (CVRCON<5>) takes the ladder supply from AVDD/AVSS or from VREF+ and VREF- on RA3 and RA2. CVREN (CVRCON<7>) powers it, CVROE (CVRCON<6>) puts CVREF on its pin, and CVR<4:0> pick one of 32 levels. The settling time of the reference (Table 31-2) matters whenever CVREF is changed.

Transistors at the top and bottom of the ladder keep CVREF from reaching either rail of its source, and since CVREF is derived from the source it follows any change in it. The tested absolute accuracy is in the electrical characteristics.

operation.topic: Voltage reference in Sleep, Reset and connection
operation.text: A wake-up from Sleep by interrupt or WDT leaves CVRCON unchanged; disabling the reference saves current in Sleep. A Reset clears CVREN and CVROE, turning the reference off and disconnecting its output. The reference runs independently of the comparators; with CVROE set it appears on RA0. Enabling that output while RA0 is a digital input raises current, as does using RA0 as a digital output with CVRSS enabled. RA0 can serve as a simple D/A output, but its drive is weak and an outside buffer is needed for loads.

The HLVD module sets a voltage trip point and a direction; when the device voltage crosses the point in that direction, HLVDIF sets and, if enabled, the device takes the interrupt. HLVDCON controls it entirely and can turn it off to save current. VDIRMAG (HLVDCON<7>) = 1 detects the voltage reaching or rising past the trip point, 0 reaching or falling below it. BGVST shows the band gap references stable; IRVST shows the detector will flag at the set level (the interrupt should not be enabled before). HLVDEN (HLVDCON<4>) enables it. HLVDL<3:0> choose the limit: 0000 lowest to 1110 highest, and 1111 takes the input from the HLVDIN pin; the levels are parameter D420.

Each time the module is enabled its circuit needs time to settle; it can interrupt only after IRVST sets. A comparator checks a tap of a resistor divider on VDD against an internal reference of 1.024V typical; at the trip point the tap equals the reference and HLVDIF sets. HLVDL<3:0> pick one of 16 trip points. With HLVDL<3:0> = 1111 the comparator takes the outside input HLVDIN instead, so the trip can be placed anywhere within the valid operating voltage range.

Write the trip point to HLVDL<3:0>; set VDIRMAG for high-voltage (1) or low-voltage (0) detection; set HLVDEN; clear HLVDIF (PIR2<2>), which an earlier event may have left set; for interrupts set HLVDIE (PIE2<2>) and GIE (INTCON<7>). No interrupt occurs until IRVST is set. Before changing VDIRMAG or HLVDL<3:0>, turn the module off (HLVDEN = 0), change them and turn it back on, which avoids false events.

When enabled, the comparator and divider draw static current, given as parameter D022B (Table 31-11); the module can be enabled only briefly for each check and then turned off. Its internal reference (parameter 37) may be shared with other circuits such as the programmable Brown-out Reset. If all its users are off, the reference needs the start-up time TIRVST, independent of the device clock (parameter 37, Table 31-11), before a voltage event can be trusted; the flag is held off until then, so short excursions past the trip point during TIRVST can go undetected.

The detector suits sensing a drop below or rise above a voltage. Enabled now and then, it can sense USB attach or detach for a device running from a lower supply than USB: a rise from, for example, 3.3V to 5V means attach and the reverse detach, saving parts and an input pin. In a battery design the voltage falls over time; at the trip point VA (time TA) an interrupt lets firmware tidy up and shut down in order before the voltage leaves the valid operating range at VB, the minimum operating voltage (time TB).

An enabled HLVD keeps running in Sleep; a crossing of the trip point sets HLVDIF and wakes the device, which goes to the interrupt vector if interrupts are globally enabled. A Reset returns all registers to their Reset state and turns the module off.

A full CAN controller for CAN 1.2, 2.0A, 2.0B passive and 2.0B active, backward compatible with the CAN modules of the PIC18CXX8, PIC18FXX8 and PIC18Fxx80. It handles standard and extended data frames with 0 to 8 data bytes, remote frames (answered automatically if wished), error and overload frames, at up to 1 Mbit/s. It offers DeviceNet data-byte filtering, three operating modes (legacy, enhanced legacy, FIFO), a double-buffered receiver with two prioritized buffers, six buffers that can each be transmit or receive, three dedicated transmit buffers with priority and abort, 16 full acceptance filters linkable to the masks, two full masks plus one filter usable as a mask, wake-up with an integrated low-pass filter, a loopback self-test, interrupts for every error state, a selectable clock source, a timer link for time-stamping, and a low-power Sleep mode.

CANTX and CANRX sit on RB2 and RB3. With CANMX (CONFIG3H<0>) they move to RC6/CANTX and RC7/CANRX on the PIC18F2XK80 and PIC18F4XK80, and to RE5/CANTX and RE4/CANRX on the PIC18F6XK80. In normal mode the module takes over the CANTX TRIS bit; the CANRX TRIS bit must be set by firmware.

Set LAT and TRIS for the CAN pins; put the module in Configuration mode; choose the functional mode; load the baud rate registers; load the filters and masks; then request normal mode or whichever mode the application needs.

Writing CANCON = 80h requests Configuration mode. The switch waits until the bus is idle, while other requests such as Loopback or Disable may take effect at once, so firmware polls the OPMODE bits in CANSTAT until they show the new mode.

operation.topic: Buffer access through the WIN bits
operation.text: The CANCON WIN bits map any transmit or receive buffer onto the RXB0 address window in the access bank. An interrupt handler can copy the CANSTAT ICODE bits into the WIN bits to reach the buffer that raised the interrupt; it first saves CANCON and CANSTAT so an access already under way and a later CAN interrupt do not disturb it, and restores the WIN bits afterwards. CANSTAT is read-only.

A transmit buffer can be written directly with banked addressing, or mapped over RXB0 with the WIN bits and written through the RXB0 names. For the standard identifier 123h, SIDH = 24h and SIDL = 60h (EXIDE = 0); the EIDH:EIDL bytes are not needed. Writing 08h to the buffer's control register requests transmission at normal priority, and TXREQ clears once the message has gone. The module must be in Normal or Loopback mode to transmit.
RXERRCNT holds the receive error count kept by the CAN rules. Above 127 the module is error-passive; this counter alone cannot take the module bus-off.

RXFUL shows that a buffer holds a message and EXID whether its identifier is extended (29 bits) or standard. After the identifier and data have been read, clearing RXFUL frees the buffer for the next message. Filters, masks and the RXM bits must be set for any message to be received.

Six modes: Configuration, Disable/Sleep, Normal, Listen Only, Loopback and Error Recognition. All but Error Recognition are requested through REQOP<2:0> (CANCON<7:5>) and confirmed by OPMODE; Error Recognition is chosen through the receive buffers' RXM bits. A mode change waits for pending transmissions to finish, so firmware checks OPMODE before going on.

Set by REQOP2 and confirmed when OPMODE2 reads high; the module returns to service when REQOP is cleared. Only in this mode can the configuration, functional mode, bit timing, filter, mask, filter/mask control and mask selection registers be written. Entry is refused while a message is being sent or received. The module neither sends nor receives, the error counters are cleared, interrupt flags are kept and the pins return to ordinary I/O.

REQOP = 001 requests it and OPMODE = 001 confirms it. The module clock stops; if a message is in progress the module first waits for 11 recessive bits (an idle bus). Pending interrupts and the error counters are kept and TXCAN stays recessive. Only the WAKIF interrupt still works: with WAKDIS clear and WAKIE set, a recessive-to-dominant edge on the bus interrupts the CPU. On wake-up the module goes back to its previous mode; the message that woke it is lost without an error frame, and if the CPU itself was asleep more than one message may be lost, depending on oscillator start-up time and bit rate. Firmware has to arrange retransmission.
The working mode: the module watches all bus traffic, sends acknowledges and error frames, and is the only mode in which it transmits.

A silent mode that receives every message, valid or not, without sending anything, not even acknowledges or error flags. It serves bus monitors and automatic baud detection on hot plugging, which needs at least two other nodes talking: trial baud rates are tried until valid messages arrive. RXM settings are ignored; filters and masks can still pass only chosen valid messages (masks of all zeros pass everything), while invalid messages always get through. The error counters are reset and stopped. Set through CANCON.

Transmit buffers feed the receive buffers internally, nothing reaching the bus; the ACK bit is ignored and the node accepts its own frames as if from another node. It is silent, TXCAN reverts to port I/O, and filters and masks still apply. Meant for development and test. Set through CANCON.

The module ignores errors and receives any message; in Mode 0 it is selected with RXM<1:0> = 11 in RXBnCON. Whatever had reached the message assembly buffer before an error is copied into the receive buffer for the CPU to read.

Mode 0 (legacy) matches the PIC18CXX8/FXX8 CAN module and is the Reset default. Mode 1 (enhanced legacy) adds six buffers B0-B5 that can be transmit or receive and answer RTR frames automatically, and 16 acceptance filters with two masks; RXF15 can act as a filter or a mask. Fourteen of the filters can be tied freely to any receive buffer and mask, so several filters can serve one buffer. With standard identifiers part of a filter can filter data bytes, 0 to 18 bits long, which suits protocols such as DeviceNet.

The receive buffers form a FIFO and any enabled filter linked to it can accept a message. Depth is 2 to 8 buffers, ending at the first programmable buffer set as transmit: with B2 as transmit, the FIFO is RXB0, RXB1, B0 and B1 (4 deep); with all of B0-B5 receiving it is 8 deep.

Three dedicated transmit buffers (TXB0-TXB2), two dedicated receive buffers (RXB0, RXB1) and, in Modes 1 and 2, six programmable buffers B0-B5. Each takes 14 bytes of SRAM mapped into the SFR space: one control register, four identifier registers (SIDH, SIDL, EIDH, EIDL), a data length count and eight data bytes. B0-B5 start as receive buffers; TXENn in BSEL0 makes one a transmit buffer, and each control register carries a bit set for each role. A message assembly buffer (MAB), not visible to firmware, always takes the next message off the bus and passes it to a receive buffer only when a filter accepts it. In Mode 2 the FIFO is read through FP<4:0> in CANCON, with no hardware guard against reading out of order.

In Modes 1 and 2 any of B0-B5 can answer a remote frame unaided: make it a transmit buffer (TXnEN in BSEL0), associate at least one filter preloaded with the expected RTR identifier, set RTREN in BnCON and preload the reply data. A matching RTR sets TXREQ and queues the buffer. While TXREQ is set the buffer is read-only and writes are ignored.

With TXREQ clear, load at least SIDH, SIDL and DLC, the data bytes if any, and EIDH:EIDL with EXIDE set for an extended identifier. Setting TXREQ clears TXABT, TXLARB and TXERR and marks the buffer ready; sending starts when the bus is free, highest priority first, and at least one node at the same baud rate must be present. On success TXREQ clears and TXBnIF sets (interrupting if TXBnIE is set). On failure TXREQ stays set and TXERR with IRXIF (error) or TXLARB (lost arbitration) is set.

Clearing a buffer's TXREQ asks to abort its message; setting ABAT (CANCON<4>) asks to abort all of them. An abort takes effect if the message has not started, or started and then lost arbitration or hit an error, and TXABT reports it; a message already being sent is finished, and if it succeeds TXABT stays clear. A message that loses arbitration or errors during an abort request is not retried. An abort request cannot be withdrawn; only the module or a POR clears it.

Before each start of frame the module compares the pending buffers and sends the one with the highest TXP setting; a tie goes to the higher-numbered buffer. TXP = 11 is the highest of the four levels, 00 the lowest. This ordering is separate from CAN bus arbitration.

An accepted message is copied whole from the MAB, overwriting every register of the receive buffer whatever its identifier type or length. RXFUL is then set and an interrupt raised if enabled; firmware clears RXFUL when done, which locks out new loads until then. Filter-hit bits (FILHIT<2:0> in Mode 0, FILHIT<4:0> in Modes 1 and 2) name the matching filter and show RTR frames; EXID tells standard (read SIDH, SIDL) from extended (also EIDH, EIDL); DLC gives the data bytes to read. RTR frames not handled automatically need a firmware reply.

RXM = 00 receives all valid messages the filters accept, the filter's EXIDE bit choosing standard or extended. In Mode 0, RXM = 01 or 10 restricts a buffer to standard or extended identifiers, and a filter whose EXIDE disagrees becomes useless; in Modes 1 and 2 the EXID bit of the SIDL mask does this. RXM = 11 (RXM1 = 1 in Modes 1 and 2) receives everything regardless of filters, including the partial content of frames cut short by an error; it is a debugging aid, not for a working system. In Modes 1 and 2 a programmable buffer set as transmit discards messages matching any filter linked to it, so no filter should be linked to a transmit buffer.

In Mode 0 RXB0 has priority, with two filters, and RXB1 has four; RXB0CON can let a message roll over into RXB1 when RXB0 is full, whatever RXB1's filters, without an overflow. Each buffer has its own mask. In Modes 1 and 2 the 16 filters link to any buffer and when several buffers match, the lowest-numbered buffer takes the message.

In Mode 2 an accepted message goes to the next free buffer and an internal write pointer advances; the FIFO is contiguous from RXB0 toward B5 and ends at the first transmit buffer (B3 as transmit gives RXB0, RXB1, B0-B2, 5 deep; B0 as transmit gives 2). Transmit buffers are best placed at the top of B0-B5. A FIFO receive sets EICODE<4:0> = 10000; FP<3:0> in CANCON point to the oldest unread buffer, and clearing its RXFUL advances them. RXFUL clear at the pointer means the FIFO is empty. FIFOWM in ECANCON can interrupt when only one or four buffers remain empty.

With CANCAP (CIOCON<4>) set, each received message sends a capture signal to CCP1 in place of its capture input, capturing Timer1 or Timer3 as a time-stamp. CCP1CON<3:0> must be 0011 to enable the special event trigger for CAN events.

Once a valid message is in the MAB its identifier is compared with the filters; a match loads it into the linked buffer. A mask bit of 1 makes that identifier bit count; a mask bit of 0 accepts the bit whatever the filter holds. In Mode 0, RXF0, RXF1 and RXM0 belong to RXB0, and RXF2-RXF5 with RXM1 to RXB1.

Ten more filters (RXF6-RXF15) give 16, each enabled by RXFENn in RXFCONn. RXFBCONn holds a nibble per filter naming its receive buffer, so one buffer can have several filters. FILn_m bits in MSELn tie each filter to a mask. Filters are checked in ascending order and the lowest-numbered match is reported. Masks and filters can only be changed in Configuration mode.

All nodes on a bus share one nominal bit rate, at most 1 Mb/s. NRZ coding carries no clock, so receivers recover it with a digital PLL, and bit stuffing guarantees an edge at least every six bits. The DPLL splits each bit into time quanta (TQ) grouped into the synchronization, propagation and two phase buffer segments. Nodes may run from different oscillator frequencies; each sets its prescaler and segment lengths to reach the common bit rate, which needs every TOSC to divide TQ exactly.

PLL-derived clocks carry phase jitter, specified at 2% (Gaussian, 3 standard deviations; parameter F13), with total jitter twice that. Over the 10 bits CAN allows without resynchronization the random error mostly cancels, leaving one jitter interval at each end. The resulting error is far below the 100 ppm (0.01%) drift typical of a crystal.

The synchronization segment, 1 TQ, is where an edge is expected. The propagation segment (1 to 8 TQ, PRSEG<2:0>) covers bus and node delays. Phase segment 1 (1 to 8 TQ) ends at the sample point and can be lengthened by resynchronization; phase segment 2 (1 to 8 TQ) delays the next transition and can be shortened. The information processing time after the sample point is fixed at 2 TQ, so phase segment 2 is at least 2 TQ, or the greater of phase segment 1 and the IPT. The sample point is best late, around 80% of the bit.
The bus is read at the end of phase segment 1. With long bit times, triple sampling takes the majority of three samples: at the sample point and at TQ/2 and TQ before it.

Hard synchronization happens only on a recessive-to-dominant edge while the bus is idle (start of a message) and restarts the bit at Sync_Seg; no resynchronization follows in that bit. Resynchronization lengthens phase segment 1 (positive phase error) or shortens phase segment 2 (negative error) by up to the SJW, 1 to 4 TQ; an error within the SJW acts like a hard synchronization. Phase error e is 0 inside Sync_Seg, positive before the sample point and negative after the previous sample point. Only recessive-to-dominant edges give timing; at most one synchronization per bit; an edge counts only if the bus value after it differs from the value at the previous sample point; a node sending a dominant bit does not resynchronize on a recessive-to-dominant edge with positive phase error.

An SJW of 1 usually suffices; a large SJW is needed only for inaccurate or unstable clocks such as ceramic resonators. Ceramic resonators are generally adequate up to 125 Kbit/s; the full CAN speed range needs a quartz oscillator (tolerances per ISO11898-1).

BRGCON1-3 can be written only in Configuration mode. BRGCON1: BRP prescaler and SJW<1:0>. BRGCON2: PRSEG, SEG1PH, SAM (1 = three samples, at TQ/2 spacing before and at the sample point, majority of two; 0 = one sample) and SEG2PHTS (1 = phase segment 2 from SEG2PH in BRGCON3; 0 = greater of phase segment 1 and the 2 TQ IPT). BRGCON3: PHSEG2<2:0>, used only when SEG2PHTS = 1.

CRC error: the received CRC disagrees with the one computed from start of frame to end of data. Acknowledge error: the transmitter finds the ACK slot still recessive. Form error: a dominant bit in end of frame, interframe space, ACK delimiter or CRC delimiter. Bit error: the bus level differs from the bit just sent, except a recessive bit overwritten during arbitration or the ACK slot. Stuff error: six equal bits in a row between start of frame and CRC delimiter. Each produces an error frame and the message is repeated.

Errors are signalled to all nodes by error frames and the failed frame is resent as soon as possible. An error-active node sends messages and dominant error frames freely; an error-passive node sends messages and recessive (passive) error frames; a bus-off node neither sends nor receives. RXERRCNT and TXERRCNT count per the CAN specification and can be read by the CPU.

Error-active below 128 on both counters, error-passive at 128 or more on either, bus-off when TXERRCNT reaches 256. Recovery takes 128 runs of 11 recessive bits and returns the module to error-active with no CPU involvement, after 128 × 11 idle bit times; the error interrupt handler can intervene if that is unwanted. COMSTAT shows the current state. EWARN sets when either counter reaches 96 and clears when both are below it.

Flags are in PIR5 and the eight main enables in PIE5, each enabled separately; the CANSTAT ICODE bits suit a jump table. Receive-side sources: receive, wake-up, receiver overrun, receiver warning, receiver error-passive. Transmit-side: transmit, transmitter warning, transmitter error-passive, bus-off. Each has one source, except the error interrupt (read COMSTAT for the cause) and, in Modes 1 and 2, one shared flag/enable for all transmit buffers and one for all receive buffers.

ICODE<3:1> (Mode 0) or EICODE<4:0> (Modes 1 and 2) in CANSTAT give the highest-priority pending enabled interrupt, lower codes being higher priority; when it clears, the next appears. In Mode 2 a receive always reads 10000 and the FIFO pointer gives the buffer.

A transmit interrupt fires when a buffer empties and can be reloaded; in Mode 0 each of TXB0-TXB2 has its own flag, cleared by the CPU. In Modes 1 and 2 all transmit buffers share one flag, firmware polls TXREQ to find the source, and individual buffers are gated by TXBnIE and BIE0. A receive interrupt fires right after end of frame of a message loaded into a buffer; Mode 0 uses RXBnIF per buffer, Mode 1 shares one flag (poll each RXFUL), and in Mode 2 it means a new message is in the FIFO.

IRXIF sets on any error while sending or receiving and interrupts if IRXIE is set; with Listen Only mode it helps find the bus baud rate. In Sleep, bus activity sets WAKIF and, if enabled, wakes the device; the CPU clears WAKIF.

With ERRIE (PIE5) set, an interrupt follows an overflow or a change of transmitter or receiver error state; COMSTAT flags the cause. Receiver overflow: the MAB holds an accepted message but its buffer is still full; RXBnOVFL sets and must be cleared by the CPU. Receiver or transmitter warning: the counter reached 96. Receiver or transmitter bus passive: the counter reached 128. Bus-off: TXERRCNT passed 255.

Oscillator selection, POR, power-up timer, oscillator start-up timer, brown-out reset, interrupts, WDT, on-chip regulator, fail-safe clock monitor, two-speed start-up, code protection, ID locations and in-circuit serial programming, all set through configuration bits. The WDT is either always on by configuration or under software control. The LF-INTOSC internal oscillator makes the clock monitor and two-speed start-up possible.

Mapped from 300000h in configuration space (300000h-3FFFFFh), beyond user program memory and reached only by table reads and writes. A programmed bit reads 0. Firmware writes them like Flash: TBLWT with TBLPTR at the register loads address and data, and setting WR in EECON1 starts a self-timed long write, one byte at a time; a TBLWT can write a 1 or a 0 into a cell.

Clocked from LF-INTOSC, which starts when the WDT is enabled; the nominal 4 ms period has the stability of that oscillator. A 16-bit postscaler chosen in CONFIG2H stretches it from 4 ms to 4,194 s, about an hour. SLEEP, CLRWDT, a change of the IRCF bits (OSCCON<6:4>) or a clock failure clear the WDT and its postscaler. WDTEN<1:0> give four modes: on, off, software control through SWDTEN (WDTCON<0>), or on while running and off in Sleep. SWDTEN works only when the configuration bits have disabled the WDT. A time-out wakes the device from power-managed modes or resets it.

REGSLP (bit 7) puts the regulator in low-power mode during Sleep (disabled on PIC18LF parts). SRETEN (bit 4, only with RETEN = 0) selects ultra low-power Sleep when set. ULPEN (bit 2) enables ultra low-power wake-up, ULPSINK (bit 1) its current sink, and ULPLVL (bit 5) reports whether RA0 is above or below about 0.5 V. SWDTEN (bit 0) turns the WDT on and has no effect when WDTEN<1:0> enable it.

The core logic runs at a nominal 3.3 V. PIC18F parts carry a normal and an ultra low-power regulator, wired alike and differing only in Sleep, so the core can run from a higher VDD such as 5 V; the regulator is on and VDDCORE/VCAP needs a low-ESR filter capacitor (value in the supply-voltage DC characteristics) for stability. On PIC18LF parts it is off, VDD feeds the core directly and must stay within VDDCORE limits, and VDDCORE/VCAP takes 0.1 µF. Below VDD = 3.3 V the regulator stops regulating and its output follows VDD down to 1.8 V; below that the output may fall to 0 V.

REGSLP (WDTCON<7>) puts the regulator in standby during Sleep for much lower current. The ultra low-power mode, set by RETEN (CONFIG1L<0>) and SRETEN (WDTCON<4>), gives the lowest current with the regulator on; it shuts the internal references, so interrupts that depend on them cannot wake the device, and an enabled BOR or LVD keeps the references on at a higher current. Wake-up from it takes about 250 µs before code runs.

With IESO set, after a Reset (following the power-up timer, if on) or a wake-up from Sleep the device runs from INTOSC (LF, MF or HF) while the primary oscillator starts and the OST counts, then switches to PRI_RUN. It is meant for LP, XT and HS crystal modes only; other sources have no OST delay. IRCF<2:0> set right after Reset, or before Sleep, give a faster clock meanwhile. Power-managed mode commands, including repeated SLEEP, still work, so code can do brief work and sleep again before the crystal is ready. OSTS (OSCCON<3>) set means the primary oscillator is clocking the device. In other power-managed modes IESO is ignored. TOST = 1024 TOSC, TPLL is about 2 ms, and the clock changeover typically takes 2 to 4 TOSC.

With FCMEN set, LF-INTOSC runs continuously; divided by 64 (488 Hz, 2.048 ms) it forms a sample clock. A latch is set by each falling edge of the device clock and cleared by each rising sample-clock edge; if a falling sample edge finds it still set, the clock has failed. Then OSCFIF (PIR2<7>) is set, the device switches to the internal oscillator (OSCCON keeps showing the old source) and the WDT is reset. Only primary and secondary clock failures are detected, not an internal oscillator failure. The postscaled internal clock may not be steady enough for timing-critical work during changeover; another clock and power-managed mode can be chosen to recover or shut down in order. The WDT and the monitor share INTOSC with separate dividers, so turning the WDT off does not stop the monitor; clock failure events reset the WDT so a slower clock does not cause a false time-out.

A Reset or entry into a power-managed mode ends it. After Reset the primary source from CONFIG1H starts, with its OST or PLL delays, INTOSC clocks the device until it is ready (OSTS set), and monitoring resumes. If the primary clock never starts, INTOSC keeps running the device and OSCCON stays at its Reset value until a power-managed mode is entered.

operation.topic: Clock monitor in power-managed modes and at start-up
operation.text: In a power-managed mode the clock chosen by OSCCON is monitored. If it fails with the interrupt enabled, INTOSC clocks the code and the device does not return to the failed clock; with the interrupt disabled, later interrupts in Idle start code running on INTOSC. After POR or wake from Sleep, EC, RC and INTOSC sources are monitored at once; crystal modes (HS, HSPLL, LP, XT) run from the internal block until the OST and PLL timers expire, so a slow start is not taken as a failure. The same logic hides an oscillator that never starts; firmware can watch OSTS with a timeout, but no failure interrupt is raised.

User program memory splits into a boot block of 1 or 2 K and blocks on binary boundaries, each with code-protect (CPx), write-protect (WRTx) and external table read (EBTRx) bits. Table reads and writes reach any program memory location, the device ID and the configuration registers. CPx bits do nothing in normal execution; they block external reads and writes. WRTx = 0 blocks table writes to a block. EBTRx = 0 lets table reads run only from inside the block; reads from outside return 0 in TABLAT. Protection bits go from 1 to 0 only; a full chip or block erase, started only through ICSP or an external programmer, sets them to 1.

CPD blocks external reads and writes of the whole data EEPROM; WRTD blocks internal and external writes. The CPU can always read the data EEPROM. WRTC write-protects the configuration registers; it is read-only in normal execution and written only through ICSP or an external programmer.
Eight locations at 200000h-200007h hold a checksum or code ID. TBLRD and TBLWT reach them in normal execution and during program/verify, and they stay readable when the device is code-protected.

The device programs in the end circuit over two lines, clock and data, plus power, ground and the programming voltage, so boards can be built blank and programmed just before shipping. DEBUG = 0 enables the in-circuit debugger, which takes RB6, RB7, two stack levels, 512 bytes of program memory and 10 bytes of data memory. Debugging needs ICSP connections to MCLR/RE3, VDD, VSS, RB7 and RB6.

The core runs the 75-instruction standard PIC18 set plus an optional extension of 8 instructions aimed at re-entrant and software-stack code. Instructions fall into byte-oriented, bit-oriented, literal and control groups. All but four are one 16-bit word; the four double-word instructions carry 1111 in the top four bits of their second word, which executes as a NOP if reached on its own.

One instruction cycle is four oscillator periods (4 MHz oscillator: 1 µs per instruction). A one-word instruction takes one cycle unless it changes the Program Counter or a conditional test is true; then it takes two, the extra cycle running as a NOP. Double-word instructions take two cycles; a taken two-word branch at 4 MHz takes 3 µs.

Byte-oriented instructions name a file register f, a destination d (0 = WREG, 1 = back to f) and an access bit a. Bit-oriented instructions name f, a bit number b and a. Literal instructions take a literal k, an FSR number f, or nothing. Control instructions take a program address n, the fast mode bit s for CALL and RETURN, or the table mode m for table reads and writes.

Byte-oriented: opcode in bits 15-10, d in bit 9, a in bit 8, 8-bit file address in bits 7-0 (ADDWF MYREG, W, B). MOVFF: opcode in bits 15-12 and a 12-bit source address, then a second word of 1111 and a 12-bit destination address. Bit-oriented: opcode in bits 15-12, bit number in bits 11-9, a in bit 8, file address in bits 7-0 (BSF MYREG, bit, B). Literal: opcode in bits 15-8, 8-bit literal in bits 7-0 (MOVLW 7Fh). GOTO: opcode in bits 15-8 and n<7:0>, then 1111 and n<19:8>, a 20-bit address. CALL: as GOTO with the fast bit S in bit 8. BRA: opcode in bits 15-11 and an 11-bit offset. Conditional branches (BC): opcode in bits 15-8 and an 8-bit offset.

With d = 0 a byte-oriented result goes to W, with d = 1 (the default) back to f. a = 0 selects the Access Bank, a = 1 the GPR bank in BSR. With the extended instruction set enabled, a = 0 and f ≤ 95 (5Fh), the instruction uses Indexed Literal Offset Addressing instead.

Conditional branches add 2n to PC + 2 when their condition holds, with n from -128 to 127; they take one cycle when not taken and two when taken. BRA and RCALL reach -1024 to 1023 words and always take two cycles. CALL and GOTO hold a 20-bit address (0 to 1048575) in two words. CALL, RETURN and RETFIE with s = 1 save or restore W, STATUS and BSR through their shadow registers; PCLATU and PCLATH are not changed by the returns.

PUSH places PC + 2 on the return stack, pushing the previous top down; POP discards the top of stack, and the value pushed before it becomes the new top. RESET resets all registers and flags a MCLR Reset affects.

TBLRD copies the program memory byte at TBLPTR into TABLAT; TBLWT copies TABLAT into the holding register. Each has four forms: pointer unchanged, post-increment, post-decrement and pre-increment. TBLPTR bit 0 picks the byte of the program word: 0 the low byte, 1 the high byte. Both take two cycles.

The extension adds eight literal instructions that work on the File Select Registers or address through them, and turns on Indexed Literal Offset Addressing for many standard instructions. It serves compiled C and other re-entrant code: allocating and freeing software stack space, calling through function pointers, moving the software stack pointer and reaching variables on the stack. ADDULNK and SUBULNK are the FSR2 forms of ADDFSR and SUBFSR that also return. The extension is on in an unprogrammed device; the XINST configuration bit enables or disables it. Indexed arguments are written in square brackets, optional ones in braces.

With the extension enabled and a = 0, a file address of 5Fh or less in a byte- or bit-oriented instruction is an offset from FSR2, not an Access Bank address; with the extension disabled the address is literal (Access Bank for a = 0, BSR bank for a = 1). About half of the standard instructions are affected, and legacy code that uses Access Bank addresses below 5Fh can read or write the wrong locations. With FSR2 = 00h the Access RAM boundaries are the original ones. In this mode the offset is written [k], k at most 5Fh, the access bit is implied 0 and not written, and d works as before; MPASM needs the /y option or the PE directive.
MPLAB IDE sets XINST = 0 by default, disabling the extension; code built for the extended set needs XINST set during programming and the extension enabled in the language tool.

Unless a table says otherwise, timing figures hold over -40°C to +85°C (industrial) or +125°C (extended) and the VDD ranges of the supply voltage and DC characteristics, with the load of load condition 1 or 2: RL = 464 Ω, CL = 50 pF on every pin except OSC2/CLKO/RA6 (PORTD and PORTE outputs used as ports included), CL = 15 pF on OSC2/CLKO/RA6.
With VDIRMAG = 1 the hardware sets HLVDIF when VDD rises through VHLVD; with VDIRMAG = 0 when VDD falls through it. Software can then clear HLVDIF.

Setting GO starts the conversion; sampling stops after a short RC delay (typically 100 ns) that also disconnects the hold capacitor from the input. The 12 result bits are produced MSb first, one per A/D clock; then ADRES takes the new value, ADIF is set and GO clears to DONE. When the A/D runs from its RC clock, the A/D clock starts one TCY late, which leaves time to execute SLEEP.

The PIC18F66K80, PIC18F4580, PIC18F4680 and PIC18F8680 families share most functions and features, so code moves to the PIC18F66K80 family with few changes. The PIC18FXX80 to PIC18FXXK80 Migration Guide (DS39982) covers the details.
